# The four-dimensional theory {#sec-csdr-four-dimensional}

The previous chapter set up coset space dimensional reduction of $SU(3)$ Yang-Mills theory over the sphere $S^2 =
SU(2)/U(1)$, with the isotropy $U(1)$ embedded along $\tau(Q_3) = \tfrac{i}{3}\operatorname{diag}(1, 1, -2)$, and found the
four-dimensional gauge group $H = SU(2) \times U(1)$ and the matching that leaves one complex doublet of scalars. This
chapter derives the four-dimensional theory itself. Solving the constraints writes the internal components of the
gauge field explicitly in terms of a Higgs doublet $\Phi = (p, q)$, shows that the solution is complete, and reduces the
higher-dimensional Yang-Mills Lagrangian to a four-dimensional gauge theory of $H$ coupled to $\Phi$. The Higgs
potential and symmetry breaking computes the internal field strength, obtains the potential $V = \tfrac12 r^2 - r +
\tfrac23$ with $r = |p|^2 + |q|^2$, finds its minimum on the sphere $r = 1$, and shows that the vacuum breaks $SU(2) \times
U(1)$ to the $U(1)$ of electromagnetism, with masses of the $W$ and $Z$ bosons and a Weinberg angle $\sin^2\theta_W =
\tfrac34$ fixed by the geometry. Both sections end with propositions, every
statement is followed by three examples and three exercises with folded solutions, and the chapter closes with three
integrative exercises, among them the Higgs mass $m_H = 2M_W$ predicted by the model. A third section,
@sec-csdr-fermions, reduces fermions over the same sphere and matches the chiral fermions it produces with the index of
@thm-monopole-index.

## Solving the constraints {#sec-csdr-solution}

The CSDR constraints of @def-csdr-constraints reduce, for the sphere, to two linear equations for the internal
components $\phi_1, \phi_2 \in \mathfrak{su}(3)$ of the gauge field. This section writes them as eigenvalue equations for
$\operatorname{ad}\tau$, solves them with the eigenspaces of @prp-csdr-eigenspaces, and obtains a complex doublet of
scalars [@kubyshin2003, Sec. 4; @kapetanakis1992]. It then substitutes the solution into the higher-dimensional
Yang-Mills Lagrangian to obtain the four-dimensional Lagrangian: a Yang-Mills field of $H = SU(2) \times U(1)$, the
doublet with its covariant derivative, and a potential that comes from the internal field strength. It has four
subsections: the constraint equations, the doublet, the reduced Lagrangian, and the properties of the
solution.

### The constraint equations

On the sphere the isotropy algebra is one-dimensional and the tangent space two-dimensional, so the constraints are
two matrix equations. The definition below writes them down, together with their complex form, which turns them into
the eigenvalue problem already solved in the previous chapter.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-csd-equivariance-equations}
#### Equivariance equations

For $S^2 = SU(2)/U(1)$ with $Q_a = \sigma_a/2i$, $[Q_a, Q_b] = \epsilon_{abc}Q_c$, $\mathfrak{r} = \operatorname{span}(Q_3)$ and
$\mathfrak{k} = \operatorname{span}(Q_1, Q_2)$, the **equivariance equations** for the internal components $\phi_1, \phi_2
\in \mathfrak{su}(3)$ are
$$
[\tau, \phi_1] = \phi_2, \qquad [\tau, \phi_2] = -\phi_1, \qquad \phi_3 = \tau ,
$$ {#eq-csd-equivariance}
the constraints 2 and 3 of @def-csdr-constraints with $f_{31}{}^2 = 1$, $f_{32}{}^1 = -1$ (@exr-csd-constraint-sphere). In
terms of $\phi_\pm = \phi_1 \mp i\phi_2$ they read $[\tau, \phi_\pm] = \pm i\phi_\pm$ [@kubyshin2003, eq. 22].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The complex form is obtained by adding and subtracting the two real equations. The first example carries out this
step, which turns the pair of real equations into two eigenvalue equations.

::: {#exm-csd-eq-complex}
#### From real to complex form

$[\tau, \phi_1 - i\phi_2] = \phi_2 + i\phi_1 = i(\phi_1 - i\phi_2)$ and $[\tau, \phi_1 + i\phi_2] = \phi_2 - i\phi_1 = -i(\phi_1 +
i\phi_2)$. Conversely, from $[\tau, \phi_\pm] = \pm i\phi_\pm$ and $\phi_1 = \tfrac12(\phi_+ + \phi_-)$, $\phi_2 = \tfrac{i}{2}(\phi_+ -
\phi_-)$ one recovers @eq-csd-equivariance. So $\phi_+ \in \mathfrak{g}_{+i}$ and $\phi_- \in \mathfrak{g}_{-i}$ in the notation of
@eq-csdr-eigenspaces.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** This step is the statement `constraints_iff_eigen` in `KaluzaKlein/CSDR/Constraints.lean`.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The equations say that $\operatorname{ad}\tau$ acts on the pair $(\phi_1, \phi_2)$ as the isotropy rotation acts on the tangent
plane. The second example makes the geometric meaning explicit.

::: {#exm-csd-eq-rotation}
#### A rotation in the tangent plane

Exponentiating, $e^{\alpha\operatorname{ad}\tau}\phi_1 = \cos\alpha\,\phi_1 + \sin\alpha\,\phi_2$ and $e^{\alpha\operatorname{ad}\tau}\phi_2 = -
\sin\alpha\,\phi_1 + \cos\alpha\,\phi_2$: conjugating the scalars by $e^{\alpha\tau}$ rotates them by the angle $\alpha$, exactly
as the isotropy rotation $e^{\alpha Q_3}$ rotates the frame $(Q_1, Q_2)$. A rotation of the sphere about the pole is undone
by a gauge transformation, which is the definition of a symmetric field.
:::

The same equations with $SU(2)$ in place of $SU(3)$ give the smaller model of @exm-rules-su2. The third example solves
them there, as a preview of the solution below.

::: {#exm-csd-eq-su2}
#### The $SU(2)$ model

For $G = SU(2)$ and $\tau = Q_3$, the $+i$ eigenspace of $\operatorname{ad}Q_3$ on $2 \times 2$ matrices is spanned by $E_{21}$
(@exr-csdr-su2-example), so $\phi_+ = fE_{21}$ with one complex number $f$, and $\phi_- = -\bar fE_{12}$. The internal field
strength is $F_{12} = [\phi_1, \phi_2] - Q_3$, proportional to $(|f|^2 - 1)\sigma_3$ [@kubyshin2003, eqs. 33-36].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise verifies the structure constants used in the definition. The constant $f_{12}{}^3$ will reappear in
the internal field strength of the next section.

::: {#exr-csd-eq-structure}
#### The structure constants of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$

Check $[Q_a, Q_b] = \epsilon_{abc}Q_c$ for $Q_a = \sigma_a/2i$, read off $f_{31}{}^2$, $f_{32}{}^1$ and $f_{12}{}^3$, and show that
$Q_\pm = Q_1 \mp iQ_2$ have charges $\pm1$ under $\operatorname{ad}Q_3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[Q_3, Q_1] = Q_2$, $[Q_3, Q_2] = -Q_1$ and $[Q_1, Q_2] = Q_3$, so $f_{31}{}^2 = 1$, $f_{32}{}^1 = -1$, $f_{12}{}^3 = 1$;
$Q_+ = -iE_{21}$ and $Q_- = -iE_{12}$ satisfy $[Q_3, Q_\pm] = \pm iQ_\pm$:

{{< sage exr-csd-eq-structure >}}
:::

The second exercise proves the equivalence of @exm-csd-eq-complex in both directions. It is a short computation with the
linearity of the commutator.

::: {#exr-csd-eq-equivalence}
#### Real and complex forms are equivalent

Show that the pair of real equations @eq-csd-equivariance holds if and only if $[\tau, \phi_+] = i\phi_+$ and $[\tau,
\phi_-] = -i\phi_-$, for arbitrary complex matrices $\phi_1, \phi_2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If the real equations hold, the computation of @exm-csd-eq-complex gives the complex ones. Conversely, adding the complex
equations gives $[\tau, \phi_+ + \phi_-] = i(\phi_+ - \phi_-)$, i.e. $2[\tau, \phi_1] = i(-2i\phi_2) = 2\phi_2$, and subtracting them
gives $[\tau, \phi_+ - \phi_-] = i(\phi_+ + \phi_-)$, i.e. $-2i[\tau, \phi_2] = 2i\phi_1$, so $[\tau, \phi_2] = -\phi_1$. No reality
condition is used, which is why the equivalence holds for all complex matrices.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `constraints_iff_eigen` in `KaluzaKlein/CSDR/Constraints.lean` holds for all complex matrices $A, B$.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The third exercise brings in the reality condition. The fields are elements of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$, and this relates $\phi_-$ to
$\phi_+$.

::: {#exr-csd-eq-reality}
#### The reality condition

Show that if $\phi_1, \phi_2$ are anti-Hermitian then $\phi_- = -\phi_+^\dagger$, and conversely that for any $\phi_+$ the
matrices $\phi_1 = \tfrac12(\phi_+ - \phi_+^\dagger)$ and $\phi_2 = \tfrac{i}{2}(\phi_+ + \phi_+^\dagger)$ are anti-Hermitian.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\phi_+^\dagger = \phi_1^\dagger + i\phi_2^\dagger = -\phi_1 - i\phi_2 = -\phi_-$. Conversely, $\phi_1^\dagger = \tfrac12(\phi_+^\dagger - \phi_+)
= -\phi_1$ and $\phi_2^\dagger = -\tfrac{i}{2}(\phi_+^\dagger + \phi_+) = -\phi_2$. With $\phi_- = -\phi_+^\dagger$ these are the
formulas $\phi_1 = \tfrac12(\phi_+ + \phi_-)$, $\phi_2 = \tfrac{i}{2}(\phi_+ - \phi_-)$. If $\phi_+ \in \mathfrak{g}_{+i}$ then $\phi_+^\dagger
\in \mathfrak{g}_{-i}$ by @exr-csd-eigen-minus, so the second complex equation follows from the first: only one complex
condition is independent.
:::
::::

### The doublet

With the eigenspaces of @prp-csdr-eigenspaces the complex equation is solved at once. The definition below names the
solution and the field that parametrises it.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-csd-higgs-doublet}
#### Higgs doublet

The general solution of @eq-csd-equivariance in $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ is
$$
\phi_+ = pE_{13} + qE_{23}, \qquad \phi_- = -\phi_+^\dagger, \qquad \phi_1 = \tfrac12(\phi_+ + \phi_-), \qquad \phi_2 =
\tfrac{i}{2}(\phi_+ - \phi_-) ,
$$ {#eq-csd-doublet}
with $(p, q) \in \mathbb{C}^2$ arbitrary functions on $M_4$. The column $\Phi = (p, q)^T$ is the **Higgs doublet** of the
model, and $r = |\Phi|^2 = |p|^2 + |q|^2$ its squared norm [@kapetanakis1992; @manton1979].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Written out, the two real fields are sparse matrices with entries only in the third row and column. The first example
displays them, as also drawn in @fig-csdr-solution.

::: {#exm-csd-doublet-matrices}
#### The matrices $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$

$$
\phi_1 = \frac12\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & p \\ 0 & 0 & q \\ -\bar p & -\bar q & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
\phi_2 = \frac{i}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & p \\ 0 & 0 & q \\ \bar p & \bar q & 0 \end{pmatrix} .
$$
Both are anti-Hermitian and traceless, and they are the real and imaginary parts, in the sense of
@exr-csd-eq-reality, of the single complex matrix $\phi_+$.
:::

The name doublet refers to how the four-dimensional gauge group acts. The second example computes this action from the
commutators with the generators of $H$.

::: {#exm-csd-doublet-action}
#### How $H$ acts

For $X = \operatorname{diag}(U, u) \in \mathfrak{h}$, with $U$ a $2 \times 2$ anti-Hermitian matrix and $u = -\operatorname{tr}U$,
$[X, \phi_+] = ((U - u)\Phi)_1E_{13} + ((U - u)\Phi)_2E_{23}$: the $SU(2)$ generators $T_a = \tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_a$ act on $\Phi$
by matrix multiplication, and $\tau$ acts as multiplication by $i$, charge $1$. $\Phi$ is a doublet of $SU(2)$ with a
$U(1)$ charge, as in the Standard Model (@exm-covariant-doublet).
:::

The count of real fields confirms that nothing has been lost. The third example compares it with the dimension of
the solution space.

::: {#exm-csd-doublet-count}
#### Four real scalars

$(p, q) \in \mathbb{C}^2$ is four real fields, and the constraint system on the sixteen real components of $(\phi_1,
\phi_2)$ has rank $12$ (@fig-csdr-solution): the solution space is four-dimensional, so @eq-csd-doublet is the general
solution, as @prp-csd-doublet-solution states.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** The statement `solution_is_doublet` in `KaluzaKlein/CSDR/Constraints.lean`.

**Sage.** The rank is computed in `figures/csdr_solution.sage` (@fig-csdr-solution).
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}

The first exercise computes the action of $H$ on the doublet in Sage. It also identifies the electric charges of the two
components, anticipating the symmetry breaking of the next section.

::: {#exr-csd-doublet-transform}
#### The doublet representation

Compute $[T_a, \phi_+]$ for $T_a = \tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_a$ in the upper block, $[\tau, \phi_+]$ and $[Q_{em}, \phi_+]$ with
$Q_{em} = \tfrac{i}{3}\operatorname{diag}(2, -1, -1)$, and express them as operations on $\Phi$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[T_a, \phi_+] \leftrightarrow T_a\Phi$, $[\tau, \phi_+] \leftrightarrow i\Phi$ and $[Q_{em}, \phi_+] \leftrightarrow (ip, 0)$: the upper
component $p$ has electric charge $1$ and the lower component $q$ is neutral.

{{< sage exr-csd-doublet-transform >}}
:::

The second exercise uses the gauge symmetry to simplify the doublet. Every doublet can be rotated into a standard form,
which will be the form of the vacuum.

::: {#exr-csd-doublet-gauge}
#### A standard form

Show that for every $\Phi \neq 0$ there is $U \in SU(2)$ with $U\Phi = (0, |\Phi|)^T$. What is the stabiliser of $(0, 1)^T$
in $SU(2)$, and in $U(2) \cong H$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$SU(2)$ acts transitively on the unit sphere $S^3 \subset \mathbb{C}^2$ (@exm-coset-s3): the matrix
$U = \frac{1}{|\Phi|}\begin{pmatrix} q & -p \\ \bar p & \bar q \end{pmatrix}$ has orthonormal rows and determinant
$(|q|^2 + |p|^2)/|\Phi|^2 = 1$, and $U\Phi = (qp - pq, |p|^2 + |q|^2)^T/|\Phi| = (0, |\Phi|)^T$. The stabiliser of $(0, 1)^T$ in $SU(2)$ is
trivial (an $SU(2)$ matrix with second column $(0, 1)^T$ is the identity). In $U(2)$, where $\tau$ acts by the phase
$e^{i\alpha}$ on both components and $SU(2)$ can compensate on the lower one, the stabiliser is a $U(1)$: it is generated
by $Q_{em}$, as found in @sec-csdr-potential.
:::

The third exercise checks the counting of @exm-csd-doublet-count by hand. It solves the real linear system without the
eigenspace decomposition.

::: {#exr-csd-doublet-rank}
#### The rank of the constraint system

Write $\phi_1 = \sum_k a_k\,i\lambda_k$, $\phi_2 = \sum_k b_k\,i\lambda_k$ and use the matrix of $\operatorname{ad}\tau$ found in
@exr-csd-embedding-gellmann to show that the constraints leave exactly $a_4, a_5, a_6, a_7$ free, with $b$ determined by $a$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\operatorname{ad}\tau$ kills $i\lambda_{1,2,3,8}$ and maps $i\lambda_4 \mapsto -i\lambda_5$, $i\lambda_5 \mapsto i\lambda_4$,
$i\lambda_6 \mapsto -i\lambda_7$, $i\lambda_7 \mapsto i\lambda_6$. The equation $[\tau, \phi_2] = -\phi_1$ forces the components
$a_{1,2,3,8}$ to vanish, and $[\tau, \phi_1] = \phi_2$ determines $b$: $b_4 = a_5$, $b_5 = -a_4$, $b_6 = a_7$, $b_7 = -a_6$,
$b_{1,2,3,8} = 0$; then the second equation holds automatically. Four free real parameters remain, matching the basis
printed by `csdr_solution.sage` and the four real components of $(p, q)$.
:::
::::

### The reduced Lagrangian

The solution is substituted into the higher-dimensional Yang-Mills Lagrangian. The definition below gives the
four-dimensional Lagrangian that results, in the normalisation used throughout this chapter.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-csd-reduced-lagrangian}
#### Reduced Lagrangian

With the six-dimensional Lagrangian $\tfrac{1}{g^2}\cdot\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}(\hat F_{MN}\hat F^{MN})$ (@def-yang-mills-action), the
signature $(+,-,-,-,-,-)$, the internal metric $R^2\delta_{ab}$ in the frame of @exr-csd-local-form-sphere, and the
symmetric field @eq-csd-doublet, the **reduced Lagrangian** is
$$
\mathcal{L}_4 = \frac{1}{g^2}\left[\frac12\operatorname{Tr}(F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}) - \frac{1}{R^2}\sum_{a=1}^{2}\operatorname{Tr}(D_\mu\phi_a
D^\mu\phi_a) - \frac{1}{R^4}V\right], \qquad V = -\operatorname{Tr}(F_{12}F_{12}) ,
$$ {#eq-csd-reduced-lagrangian}
with $A_\mu \in \mathfrak{h}$, $D_\mu\phi_a = \partial_\mu\phi_a + [A_\mu, \phi_a]$ and the internal field strength $F_{12}$ of
@def-csd-internal-field-strength; it agrees with @manolakos2016 [eqs. 10-11] and @manousselis2000 [eqs. 17-18] up to
the normalisation of the trace and the sign conventions noted there.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The kinetic term of the scalars is the familiar kinetic term of a complex doublet. The first example states the
identity behind this, checked in @exr-csd-lagr-kinetic.

::: {#exm-csd-lagr-kinetic}
#### The scalar kinetic term

$-\sum_a\operatorname{Tr}(\phi_a\phi_a) = |p|^2 + |q|^2 = \Phi^\dagger\Phi$, and $D_\mu\phi_a$ is again of the form
@eq-csd-doublet with $\Phi$ replaced by $D_\mu\Phi = \partial_\mu\Phi + A^a_\mu T_a\Phi + iA^4_\mu\Phi$ (where $A_\mu = A^a_\mu T_a +
A^4_\mu\tau$). So $-\sum_a\operatorname{Tr}(D_\mu\phi_aD^\mu\phi_a) = (D_\mu\Phi)^\dagger D^\mu\Phi$: the doublet is minimally coupled
to the gauge fields of $H$.
:::

The three terms come from the three types of components of $\hat F_{MN}$. The second example shows where each comes
from.

::: {#exm-csd-lagr-split}
#### Where the terms come from

$\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}(\hat F_{MN}\hat F^{MN})$ splits into $\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}(F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu})$, the mixed terms
$\operatorname{Tr}(F_{\mu a}F^{\mu a})$ with $F_{\mu a} = D_\mu\phi_a$ and $g^{ab} = -\delta^{ab}/R^2$, and the internal part
$\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}(F_{ab}F^{ab}) = \tfrac{1}{R^4}\operatorname{Tr}(F_{12}F_{12})$ (the two orderings $(1,2)$ and $(2,1)$
contribute equally). The internal part, with its sign, is minus the potential.
:::

The sign of the potential deserves a check, since conventions vary in the literature. The third example verifies that
the potential defined here is non-negative and enters the Lagrangian with the correct sign.

::: {#exm-csd-lagr-sign}
#### The sign of the potential

For an anti-Hermitian matrix $X$, $-\operatorname{Tr}(X^2) = \operatorname{Tr}(X^\dagger X) \geq 0$, with equality only for $X = 0$.
So $V \geq 0$ and, in the signature $(+,-,-,-)$ of @sec-conventions-indices, the Lagrangian has the form kinetic
minus potential, $\mathcal{L} = \tfrac12\dot\varphi^2 - \dots - V$ (@def-lagrangian-density). The papers cited write $+V$
with an opposite trace convention [@manolakos2016, eq. 10].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise derives the split of @exm-csd-lagr-split in detail. It is the same bookkeeping as in the reduction
of Part III, with a non-abelian field and a curved internal space.

::: {#exr-csd-lagr-split}
#### Splitting the Yang-Mills Lagrangian

With $\hat A = A_\mu dx^\mu + (\text{internal part})$ and frame indices $a, b$ on the sphere, show that
$\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}(\hat F_{MN}\hat F^{MN}) = \tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}(F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}) + \operatorname{Tr}(F_{\mu a}F^{\mu a}) +
\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}(F_{ab}F^{ab})$, and evaluate the last two terms with $g^{ab} = -\delta^{ab}/R^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The double sum over $M, N$ splits into $(\mu, \nu)$, $(\mu, a)$ and $(a, \mu)$, which are equal and give the factor $1$,
and $(a, b)$. With the block-diagonal metric, $F^{\mu a} = \eta^{\mu\nu}g^{ab}F_{\nu b} = -\tfrac{1}{R^2}F^\mu{}_a$, so
$\operatorname{Tr}(F_{\mu a}F^{\mu a}) = -\tfrac{1}{R^2}\sum_a\operatorname{Tr}(D_\mu\phi_aD^\mu\phi_a)$, using $F_{\mu a} = \partial_\mu\phi_a +
[A_\mu, \phi_a]$ for $y$-independent frame components. The internal term is $\tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac{1}{R^4}(\operatorname{Tr}
F_{12}^2 + \operatorname{Tr}F_{21}^2) = \tfrac{1}{R^4}\operatorname{Tr}F_{12}^2$. Multiplying by $1/g^2$ gives
@eq-csd-reduced-lagrangian; the volume of the sphere has been absorbed into $g$.
:::

The second exercise verifies the kinetic identity of @exm-csd-lagr-kinetic in Sage. It is a polarisation identity for the
real inner product $-\operatorname{Tr}(XY)$ on doublet fields.

::: {#exr-csd-lagr-kinetic}
#### The kinetic term in Sage

For two doublet fields built from $\Phi = (p, q)$ and $\Psi = (u, v)$ by @eq-csd-doublet, show $-\sum_a\operatorname{Tr}(\phi_a\psi_a) =
\operatorname{Re}(\Phi^\dagger\Psi)$, and check that $[A, \phi_a]$ for $A \in \mathfrak{h}$ is the doublet field of $(A^aT_a +
iA^4)\Phi$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Both identities hold for all values of the fields; together they give $-\sum_a\operatorname{Tr}(D_\mu\phi_aD^\mu\phi_a) =
(D_\mu\Phi)^\dagger D^\mu\Phi$:

{{< sage exr-csd-lagr-kinetic >}}
:::

The third exercise is about scales. It identifies the canonically normalised fields and the dimensions of the couplings
that appear in @eq-csd-reduced-lagrangian.

::: {#exr-csd-lagr-scales}
#### Canonical normalisation

Rescale $A_\mu \to gA_\mu$ and $\Phi \to gRH$ in @eq-csd-reduced-lagrangian. Show that the gauge and Higgs kinetic terms
become canonical, and write the potential in terms of $H$. Which combinations of $g$ and $R$ play the roles of the
quartic coupling and of the mass parameter?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\tfrac{1}{g^2}\cdot\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}(F F) \to \tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}(FF) = -\tfrac14F^a_{\mu\nu}F^{a\mu\nu}$ (with
$\operatorname{Tr}(T_aT_b) = -\tfrac12\delta_{ab}$), the commutator terms acquiring the coupling $g$; the scalar term becomes
$\tfrac{1}{g^2R^2}(gR)^2|D_\mu H|^2 = |D_\mu H|^2$. With $V = \tfrac12r^2 - r + \tfrac23$ (@prp-csd-potential) and $r = g^2R^2 |
H|^2$, $\tfrac{1}{g^2R^4}V = \tfrac{g^2}{2}|H|^4 - \tfrac{1}{R^2}|H|^2 + \tfrac{2}{3g^2R^4}$: a quartic coupling $\lambda = g^2/2$
fixed by the gauge coupling, a negative mass term $-\mu^2|H|^2$ with $\mu = 1/R$ fixed by the size of the sphere, and a
constant. Nothing is adjustable: this is the predictive power of the method (@exr-csd-int-higgs-mass).
:::
::::

### Worked computations

The solution of the constraints and its properties are finite computations with $3 \times 3$ matrices. The proposition
below collects them, as checked by the script that draws @fig-csdr-solution.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-csd-doublet-solution}
#### The doublet solves the constraints

For all $(p, q) \in \mathbb{C}^2$ the fields @eq-csd-doublet are anti-Hermitian, traceless and satisfy @eq-csd-equivariance;
the solution space of @eq-csd-equivariance in $\mathfrak{su}(3) \times \mathfrak{su}(3)$ is four-dimensional and is spanned by
them; $-\operatorname{Tr}(\phi_1^2 + \phi_2^2) = |p|^2 + |q|^2$; $[\phi_1, \phi_2] = \tfrac{i}{2}\operatorname{diag}(\Phi\Phi^\dagger, -
|\Phi|^2)$ in block form; and $\mathfrak{h}$ acts on $\phi_+$ as on the doublet $\Phi$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending; see @exm-csd-sol-lean for the related statements.

**Sage.** Checked by exact computation in `figures/csdr_solution.sage`.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The bracket formula is the key input for the potential of the next section. The first example evaluates it at the
point that will turn out to be the vacuum.

::: {#exm-csd-sol-bracket-point}
#### The bracket at a point

For $\Phi = (0, 1)$: $\phi_1 = \tfrac12(E_{23} - E_{32})$, $\phi_2 = \tfrac{i}{2}(E_{23} + E_{32})$ and $[\phi_1, \phi_2] =
\tfrac{i}{2}\operatorname{diag}(0, 1, -1)$, which is $\tfrac{i}{2}$ times the block matrix $\operatorname{diag}(\Phi\Phi^\dagger, -1)$
with $\Phi\Phi^\dagger = \operatorname{diag}(0, 1)$.
:::

The norm identity says that the doublet has the standard kinetic normalisation. The second example illustrates it on a
sample configuration.

::: {#exm-csd-sol-norm}
#### A sample norm

For $p = 0.6 + 0.3i$ and $q = 0.8 - 0.2i$, $|p|^2 + |q|^2 = 0.45 + 0.68 = 1.13$, and $-\operatorname{Tr}(\phi_1^2 + \phi_2^2)$ gives the same number: each of $\phi_1$, $\phi_2$ contributes
half, $-\operatorname{Tr}\phi_1^2 = -\operatorname{Tr}\phi_2^2 = \tfrac12 r$.
:::

The proposition bundles statements of different kinds. The third example separates them into existence, completeness
and the algebraic facts used later.

::: {#exm-csd-sol-lean}
#### Existence, completeness and algebra

The proposition contains an existence statement (the doublet @eq-csd-doublet satisfies @eq-csd-equivariance), a
completeness statement (every solution is of this form, the dimension count of @exm-csd-doublet-count), a reality
statement (the doublet fields are anti-Hermitian and traceless) and the equivalence of the real equations with the
eigenvalue equations of @exm-csd-eq-complex. The trace and bracket formulas are the algebraic facts used for the
potential in the next section.
:::

**Lean.** The file `KaluzaKlein/CSDR/Constraints.lean` states the same facts as `doublet_solves` (the doublet satisfies
@eq-csd-equivariance), `solution_is_doublet` (every solution is of this form), `doublet_antihermitian` and
`constraints_iff_eigen` (@exm-csd-eq-complex). These are not yet part of the verification of this chapter.

**Sage.** The proposition relies on the computation in `figures/csdr_solution.sage`.
