:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise recovers the doublet from the fields. This inverse map is what identifies the four real scalars with
$\Phi$.

::: {#exr-csd-sol-inverse}
#### From $(\phi_1, \phi_2)$ back to $\Phi$

Given a solution $(\phi_1, \phi_2)$ of @eq-csd-equivariance in $\mathfrak{su}(3)$, show that $p = (\phi_1 - i\phi_2)_{13}$ and $q =
(\phi_1 - i\phi_2)_{23}$, and that $p = 2(\phi_1)_{13}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\phi_1 - i\phi_2 = \phi_+ = pE_{13} + qE_{23}$ by @exm-csd-eq-complex, so its $(1,3)$ and $(2,3)$ entries are $p$ and $q$. From
@exm-csd-doublet-matrices, $(\phi_1)_{13} = p/2$ and $(\phi_2)_{13} = ip/2$, so $(\phi_1 - i\phi_2)_{13} = p/2 + p/2 = p$, consistent.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** This is the formula used in `solution_is_doublet` in `KaluzaKlein/CSDR/Constraints.lean`.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The second exercise computes the commutators of the doublet fields in both the real and the complex form. The result
lies in the gauge algebra, as the grading of @exr-csd-eigen-grading predicts.

::: {#exr-csd-sol-bracket}
#### Commutators of the doublet fields

Compute $[\phi_+, \phi_-]$ and $[\phi_1, \phi_2]$, check $[\phi_1, \phi_2] = -\tfrac{i}{2}[\phi_+, \phi_-]$, and verify that both
commute with $\tau$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[\phi_+, \phi_-] = -\operatorname{diag}(\Phi\Phi^\dagger, -|\Phi|^2)$ in block form; then $[\phi_1, \phi_2] = \tfrac{i}{4}[\phi_+ +
\phi_-, \phi_+ - \phi_-] = -\tfrac{i}{2}[\phi_+, \phi_-]$, and both are block diagonal, so they lie in the kernel of
$\operatorname{ad}\tau$:

{{< sage exr-csd-sol-bracket >}}
:::

The third exercise compares with the $SU(2)$ model. The structure is the same, with a single complex number in place of
the doublet.

::: {#exr-csd-sol-su2}
#### The $SU(2)$ analogue

For $G = SU(2)$, $\tau = Q_3$ and $\phi_+ = fE_{21}$, compute $\phi_1$, $\phi_2$, $-\operatorname{Tr}(\phi_1^2 + \phi_2^2)$ and
$[\phi_1, \phi_2]$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\phi_- = -\bar fE_{12}$, $\phi_1 = \tfrac12(fE_{21} - \bar fE_{12})$, $\phi_2 = \tfrac{i}{2}(fE_{21} + \bar fE_{12})$. Then
$\phi_1^2 = -\tfrac14|f|^2\mathbb{1}$, $\phi_2^2 = -\tfrac14|f|^2\mathbb{1}$, so $-\operatorname{Tr}(\phi_1^2 + \phi_2^2) = |f|^2$, and
$[\phi_1, \phi_2] = \tfrac{i}{2}|f|^2\operatorname{diag}(-1, 1) = -\tfrac{i}{2}|f|^2\sigma_3 = |f|^2 Q_3$. With $\phi_3 = Q_3$ the
internal field strength is $(|f|^2 - 1)Q_3$ and the potential $-\operatorname{Tr}F_{12}^2 = \tfrac12(|f|^2 - 1)^2$, as in
@exr-csdr-su2-example.
:::
::::

## The Higgs potential and symmetry breaking {#sec-csdr-potential}

The reduced Lagrangian @eq-csd-reduced-lagrangian contains a potential for the Higgs doublet, coming from the internal
components of the higher-dimensional field strength. Unlike in the Standard Model, where the potential is put in by
hand, its form here is fixed by the coset and the embedding, and for a symmetric coset it necessarily breaks the
four-dimensional gauge group [@manousselis2000, Sec. 3; @kapetanakis1992]. This section computes the internal field
strength and the potential, finds the vacuum and the unbroken electromagnetic $U(1)$, and obtains the masses of the
gauge bosons and the Weinberg angle of the model of Manton [@manton1979]. It has six subsections: the internal field
strength, the potential, the vacuum, the electric charge, the Weinberg angle, and the results.

### The internal field strength

The potential is the square of the internal components of the field strength. The definition below gives these
components on the symmetric field, where the structure constants of the coset enter through the fixed component
$\phi_3 = \tau$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-csd-internal-field-strength}
#### Internal field strength

The **internal field strength** of the symmetric field on $S^2$ is
$$
F_{12} = [\phi_1, \phi_2] - f_{12}{}^C\phi_C = [\phi_1, \phi_2] - \tau ,
$$ {#eq-csd-f12}
since $f_{12}{}^3 = 1$ and $\phi_3 = \tau$ (@exr-csd-eq-structure) [@manolakos2016, eq. 11; @kubyshin2003, eq. 36]. It is an
element of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ that depends on $x$ only through $\Phi$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
By @prp-csd-doublet-solution the commutator is block diagonal, and so is $F_{12}$. The first example writes it in block
form, which is all that is needed for the potential.

::: {#exm-csd-fs-block}
#### Block form

With $[\phi_1, \phi_2] = \tfrac{i}{2}\operatorname{diag}(\Phi\Phi^\dagger, -|\Phi|^2)$ and $\tau = \tfrac{i}{2}\operatorname{diag}(\tfrac23\mathbb{1}_2, -
\tfrac43)$,
$$
F_{12} = \frac{i}{2}\begin{pmatrix} \Phi\Phi^\dagger - \tfrac23\mathbb{1}_2 & 0 \\ 0 & -|\Phi|^2 + \tfrac43 \end{pmatrix} ,
$$
an element of the centraliser algebra $\mathfrak{h}$, as it must be by the grading of @exr-csd-eigen-grading.
:::

At the symmetric point $\Phi = 0$ the internal field is the embedded monopole alone. The second example describes it.

::: {#exm-csd-fs-zero}
#### The symmetric point

At $\Phi = 0$, $F_{12} = -\tau$: the internal field strength is that of a monopole on $S^2$ embedded in $SU(3)$ along $\tau$,
the field $\tau(\theta^3Q_3)$ of @exr-csd-local-form-sphere, whose curvature is $-\tau$ times the area form. The whole gauge
group $H$ is unbroken there.
:::

On the sphere $|\Phi| = 1$ the field strength takes a particularly simple form. The third example evaluates it at the point
$\Phi = (0, 1)$, which will be the vacuum.

::: {#exm-csd-fs-vacuum}
#### At the vacuum

At $\Phi = (0, 1)$, $\Phi\Phi^\dagger = \operatorname{diag}(0, 1)$ and $F_{12} = \tfrac{i}{2}\operatorname{diag}(-\tfrac23, \tfrac13, \tfrac13) = -
\tfrac12Q_{em}$ with $Q_{em} = \tfrac{i}{3}\operatorname{diag}(2, -1, -1)$: part of the monopole survives, but only along the generator
of the unbroken $U(1)$ (@def-csd-electric-charge).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise computes $F_{12}$ for a general doublet in Sage. It also evaluates the trace with $\tau$, used below to
show that $F_{12}$ never vanishes.

::: {#exr-csd-fs-explicit}
#### $F_{12}$ in Sage

Compute $F_{12}$ for $\phi_+ = pE_{13} + qE_{23}$, its values at $\Phi = 0$ and $\Phi = (0, 1)$, and $\operatorname{Tr}(\tau F_{12})$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The result is the block form of @exm-csd-fs-block, with $\operatorname{Tr}(\tau F_{12}) = \tfrac23 - \tfrac{r}{2}$:

{{< sage exr-csd-fs-explicit >}}
:::

The second exercise checks that the potential built from $F_{12}$ is gauge invariant. The argument is the same as for any
Yang-Mills field strength.

::: {#exr-csd-fs-covariance}
#### Covariance under $H$

Show that under $\phi_a \mapsto h^{-1}\phi_ah$, $h \in H$, the internal field strength transforms as $F_{12} \mapsto
h^{-1}F_{12}h$, and deduce that $\operatorname{Tr}F_{12}^2$ is invariant.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[h^{-1}\phi_1h, h^{-1}\phi_2h] = h^{-1}[\phi_1, \phi_2]h$, and $h^{-1}\tau h = \tau$ because $h$ commutes with $\tau$. So
$F_{12} \mapsto h^{-1}F_{12}h$, and the trace of the square is invariant under conjugation. The term $\tau$ in
@eq-csd-f12 is invariant only under $H$, not under all of $SU(3)$: this is how the embedding breaks $SU(3)$ to $H$ at the
level of the potential.
:::

The third exercise proves that the internal field strength never vanishes. This is why the minimum of the potential will
be positive.

::: {#exr-csd-fs-never-zero}
#### $F_{12}$ never vanishes

Using the block form, show that $F_{12} = 0$ has no solution $\Phi \in \mathbb{C}^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$F_{12} = 0$ requires $\Phi\Phi^\dagger = \tfrac23\mathbb{1}_2$. The left-hand side has rank at most one (it maps every vector to a
multiple of $\Phi$), the right-hand side rank two: impossible. Alternatively, the lower entry requires $|\Phi|^2 = \tfrac43$
and the trace of the upper block requires $|\Phi|^2 = \tfrac43$ as well, but then $\Phi\Phi^\dagger$ has eigenvalues $\tfrac43$ and $0$,
not $\tfrac23, \tfrac23$. So $V = -\operatorname{Tr}F_{12}^2 > 0$ everywhere, in contrast with the $SU(2)$ model, where
$F_{12} = (|f|^2 - 1)Q_3$ vanishes at $|f| = 1$ (@exr-csd-sol-su2).
:::
::::

### The potential

Squaring the internal field strength gives the potential of the Higgs doublet. The definition below names it, in the
normalisation of @eq-csd-reduced-lagrangian.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-csd-higgs-potential}
#### Higgs potential

The **Higgs potential** of the model is
$$
V(\Phi) = -\operatorname{Tr}(F_{12}F_{12}) = \tfrac12 r^2 - r + \tfrac23, \qquad r = |p|^2 + |q|^2 ,
$$ {#eq-csd-potential}
a quartic polynomial in the doublet, invariant under $H$ (@prp-csd-potential); the potential energy density in four
dimensions is $V/(g^2R^4)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The constant term has a direct meaning in terms of the embedded monopole. The first example evaluates the potential at
the symmetric point.

::: {#exm-csd-pot-zero}
#### The value at $\Phi = 0$

$V(0) = -\operatorname{Tr}\tau^2 = \tfrac19(1 + 1 + 4) = \tfrac23$: the energy of the embedded monopole of @exm-csd-fs-zero. The
point $\Phi = 0$ is a critical point of $V$ (a local maximum, since $\partial V/\partial r = r - 1 = -1 < 0$ there).
:::

Completing the square exhibits the minimum at once. The second example rewrites the potential in the standard
Mexican-hat form of @eq-mexican-hat.

::: {#exm-csd-pot-square}
#### The Mexican hat

$V = \tfrac12(r - 1)^2 + \tfrac16 = \tfrac12(|\Phi|^2 - 1)^2 + \tfrac16$: the potential @eq-mexican-hat with $\lambda = 2$, $\mu = 1$,
shifted by the constant $\tfrac16$. The minimum is on the sphere $|\Phi| = 1$, and the minimum value is $\tfrac16$, not $0$.
:::

The potential depends on the four real components of $\Phi$ only through $r$. The third example explains why this had
to be so.

::: {#exm-csd-pot-invariance}
#### Why only $r$ appears

$V$ is invariant under $H \cong U(2)$ acting on $\Phi \in \mathbb{C}^2$ by @exm-csd-doublet-action, and $U(2)$ acts transitively
on each sphere $|\Phi| = \text{const}$. A function on $\mathbb{C}^2$ invariant under $U(2)$ is a function of $|\Phi|^2$ alone,
and a quartic polynomial in $(p, q, \bar p, \bar q)$ invariant under $U(2)$ is a quadratic polynomial in $r$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
![The Higgs potential of $SU(3)$ over $S^2$. Left: $V(r) = \tfrac12r^2 - r + \tfrac23$ as a function of $r = |p|^2 + |
q|^2$, with the value $\tfrac23$ at the symmetric point and the minimum $\tfrac16$ at $r = 1$. Right: $V$ over the plane
$(\operatorname{Re}p, \operatorname{Re}q)$ (clipped at $1.3$), with the circle of vacua $|\Phi| = 1$. Sage checks the formula
$V = -\operatorname{Tr}F_{12}^2 = \tfrac12r^2 - r + \tfrac23$ exactly. Generated by
`figures/csdr_potential.sage`.](figures/csdr_potential.svg){#fig-csdr-potential width=95%}

{{< interactive csdr_potential 520 >}}

The interactive version shows, on the left, the surface $V$ over the $(\operatorname{Re}q, \operatorname{Im}q)$ plane at $p = 0$:
a Mexican hat whose rim, the red circle at height $\tfrac16$, is a great circle of the three-sphere of vacua. On the right
is the radial profile $V(r)$; dragging rotates the surface, and hovering reads off the values.

The first exercise derives the potential in Sage from the matrices of the previous section. It also identifies the
unbroken generator at the vacuum, anticipating the next subsections.

::: {#exr-csdr-potential}
#### The potential in Sage

Compute $[\phi_1, \phi_2]$, $F_{12}$ and $V = -\operatorname{Tr}F_{12}^2$ for the doublet, find the minimum, and determine the
diagonal generators of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ that commute with the vacuum $\phi_+ = E_{23}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-csdr-potential >}}
:::

The second exercise derives the same formula by hand from the block form. The computation is short and shows where each
term comes from.

::: {#exr-csd-pot-by-hand}
#### The potential by hand

Using @exm-csd-fs-block and $\operatorname{Tr}((\Phi\Phi^\dagger)^2) = |\Phi|^4$, compute $-\operatorname{Tr}F_{12}^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$-\operatorname{Tr}F_{12}^2 = \tfrac14\left[\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi\Phi^\dagger - \tfrac23\mathbb{1})^2 + (r - \tfrac43)^2\right]$. The first
trace is $r^2 - \tfrac43r + \tfrac89$ (using $\operatorname{Tr}\Phi\Phi^\dagger = r$), the second term $r^2 - \tfrac83r + \tfrac{16}{9}$; the
sum is $2r^2 - 4r + \tfrac{24}{9}$, and a quarter of it is $\tfrac12r^2 - r + \tfrac23$, @eq-csd-potential.
:::

The third exercise compares the three potentials met so far. The comparison shows which features are generic and which
depend on the embedding.

::: {#exr-csd-pot-compare}
#### Three models compared

Compare the potential of the running example with those of the $SU(2)$ model (@exr-csdr-su2-example) and of $SU(3)$ with the
$T_3$ embedding (@exr-csd-int-t3-model): number of scalars, minimum value, unbroken group.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$SU(2)$, $\tau = Q_3$: one complex scalar $f$, $V = \tfrac12(|f|^2 - 1)^2$, minimum $0$ at $|f| = 1$, where $F_{12} = 0$; the
$U(1)$ gauge group is broken completely. $SU(3)$, $T_3$ embedding: the same potential for one singlet $f$ (the $SU(2)$
model in the upper block), minimum $0$, and of $H = U(1)^2$ the $\lambda_8$ factor survives. $SU(3)$, $\lambda_8$
embedding: a doublet, $V = \tfrac12(r - 1)^2 + \tfrac16$, minimum $\tfrac16 > 0$, $H = SU(2) \times U(1)$ broken to $U(1)_{em}$. In
all three cases the symmetric point is unstable and the gauge group breaks spontaneously, as it must for a symmetric
coset [@manousselis2000, Sec. 3]; whether the vacuum energy vanishes depends on whether $\tau$ extends to an embedding
of all of $SU(2)$ (it does for the first two, where $\tau$ has half-integer charges, and not for the third).
:::
::::

### The vacuum

The minima of the potential form a manifold, and the choice of one point of it is the spontaneous breaking of the gauge
symmetry. The definition below names this manifold and the standard point on it.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-csd-vacuum-manifold}
#### Vacuum manifold

The **vacuum manifold** is the set of minima of $V$, $\{\Phi \in \mathbb{C}^2 : |p|^2 + |q|^2 = 1\} \cong S^3$, on which $V =
\tfrac16$ (@prp-csd-potential). By @exr-csd-doublet-gauge every vacuum is gauge equivalent to $\Phi_0 = (0, 1)$, i.e.
$\phi_+ = E_{23}$, the vacuum used from now on (@def-vacuum).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The vacuum manifold is a homogeneous space of the gauge group. The first example identifies it as a coset space, as for
any spontaneously broken symmetry (@def-unbroken-subgroup).

::: {#exm-csd-vac-coset}
#### The vacuum manifold as a coset

$H \cong U(2)$ acts transitively on $S^3$ with stabiliser $U(1)_{em}$ at $\Phi_0$, so $S^3 \cong U(2)/U(1)_{em}$. Its dimension
$3 = 4 - 1$ is the number of broken generators.
:::

Directions along the vacuum manifold cost no energy. The second example identifies them in the Hessian of the
potential, computed in @exr-csd-ppot-hessian.

::: {#exm-csd-vac-flat}
#### Flat and massive directions

In the real coordinates $(\operatorname{Re}p, \operatorname{Im}p, \operatorname{Re}q, \operatorname{Im}q)$ the Hessian of $V$ at $\Phi_0$ is
$\operatorname{diag}(0, 0, 4, 0)$: three flat directions tangent to $S^3$, the would-be Goldstone bosons (@def-goldstone-boson)
absorbed by the massive gauge bosons, and one massive radial direction, the Higgs boson.
:::

The minimum value of the potential is positive, unlike in the Standard Model. The third example interprets the field
strength that remains in the vacuum.

::: {#exm-csd-vac-monopole}
#### The vacuum carries a monopole

At $\Phi_0$, $F_{12} = -\tfrac12Q_{em}$ (@exm-csd-fs-vacuum): the vacuum is a magnetic monopole on the sphere for the unbroken
electromagnetic $U(1)$. Its energy is $V = -\tfrac14\operatorname{Tr}Q_{em}^2 = \tfrac14 \cdot \tfrac19(4 + 1 + 1) = \tfrac16$, a positive
contribution $\tfrac{1}{6g^2R^4}$ to the four-dimensional vacuum energy.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise computes the Hessian of the potential at the vacuum in Sage. It confirms the count of flat and massive
directions in @exm-csd-vac-flat.

::: {#exr-csd-ppot-hessian}
#### The Hessian at the vacuum

Compute the gradient and the Hessian of $V = \tfrac12r^2 - r + \tfrac23$ in the real coordinates of $\mathbb{C}^2$ at $(0, 0, 1, 0)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $r = \sum x_k^2$, $\partial_kV = 2(r - 1)x_k$ vanishes on $r = 1$, and $\partial_k\partial_lV = 4x_kx_l + 2(r - 1)\delta_{kl}$ is
$4$ in the radial direction and $0$ in the three tangent directions:

{{< sage exr-csd-ppot-hessian >}}
:::

The second exercise checks the claim of @exm-csd-vac-monopole at vacua other than $\Phi_0$. Since all vacua are gauge
equivalent, $F_{12}$ must be conjugate to $-\tfrac12Q_{em}$ everywhere on the vacuum manifold.

::: {#exr-csd-ppot-vacuum-f}
#### $F_{12}$ on the vacuum manifold

For several exact points $\Phi$ with $|\Phi| = 1$, compute the eigenvalues of $F_{12}$ and the value of $V$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The eigenvalues are always $\tfrac{i}{6}(-2, 1, 1)$, those of $-\tfrac12Q_{em}$, and $V = \tfrac16$:

{{< sage exr-csd-ppot-vacuum-f >}}
:::

The third exercise counts the fate of the four real scalars. It is the Higgs mechanism of @def-higgs-mechanism applied to
the model.

::: {#exr-csd-vac-goldstone}
#### Where the scalars go

Of the four real components of $\Phi$, which become massive, which are eaten, and by which gauge bosons? Use the unitary
gauge (@def-unitary-gauge).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In the unitary gauge the three tangent directions to $S^3$ at $\Phi_0$ are removed by an $H$-gauge transformation, so
$\Phi = (0, 1 + \rho)$ with $\rho$ real: one physical scalar, the Higgs boson, with the mass found in
@exr-csd-int-higgs-mass. The three removed components become the longitudinal polarisations of the three gauge bosons
that acquire mass, $W^\pm$ and $Z$ (@prp-csd-symmetry-breaking); the photon, along the unbroken $Q_{em}$, eats nothing and
stays massless.
:::
::::

### The electric charge

A vacuum is left invariant by a subgroup of the gauge group, and the gauge fields of that subgroup stay massless. The
definition below names the generator of the unbroken subgroup at $\Phi_0$, which plays the role of the electric charge.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-csd-electric-charge}
#### Electric charge

The **electric charge** of the model is the generator
$$
Q_{em} = \frac{i}{3}\operatorname{diag}(2, -1, -1) = T_3 + \tfrac12\tau, \qquad T_3 = \tfrac{i}{2}\operatorname{diag}(1, -1, 0) ,
$$ {#eq-csd-qem}
of the subgroup $U(1)_{em}$ of $H$ that leaves the vacuum $\Phi_0$ invariant (@def-unbroken-subgroup); the charge of a
field component $X$ with $[Q_{em}, X] = iQX$ is the number $Q$ (@prp-csd-symmetry-breaking).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The decomposition of $Q_{em}$ into $T_3$ and the hypercharge direction is the Gell-Mann-Nishijima relation of the Standard
Model. The first example checks it entry by entry.

::: {#exm-csd-qem-decomposition}
#### $Q_{em} = T_3 + \tfrac12\tau$

$T_3 + \tfrac12\tau = i\operatorname{diag}(\tfrac12 + \tfrac16, -\tfrac12 + \tfrac16, 0 - \tfrac13) = \tfrac{i}{3}\operatorname{diag}(2, -1, -1)$.
In terms of Hermitian charges, with the doublet's $\tau$-charge $1$ playing the role of twice the hypercharge,
$Q = T_3 + Y$ with $Y = \tfrac12$ on the doublet: the familiar formula of the electroweak theory.
:::

The charges of the doublet components follow. The second example lists them and explains why the vacuum must sit in the
neutral component.

::: {#exm-csd-qem-doublet}
#### Charges of the Higgs doublet

$[Q_{em}, \phi_+] \leftrightarrow (ip, 0)$ (@exr-csd-doublet-transform): $p$ has charge $1$ and $q$ charge $0$. The vacuum $\Phi_0 =
(0, 1)$ lies in the neutral component, as it must for $Q_{em}$ to be unbroken; a vacuum with $p \neq 0$ is gauge equivalent
to it, but breaks the conjugate $U(1)$ of @exr-csd-qem-other-vacuum.
:::

The gauge bosons and the scalars both live in the adjoint, so they are charged too. The third example computes the
charges of all eight components of the adjoint.

::: {#exm-csd-qem-adjoint}
#### Charges of the gauge bosons

With $Q_{em} = i\operatorname{diag}(q_1, q_2, q_3)$, $q = (\tfrac23, -\tfrac13, -\tfrac13)$, the unit $E_{jk}$ has charge $q_j - q_k$: $E_{12}$
and $E_{21}$ have charges $\pm1$ (the $W^\pm$ bosons, in $\mathfrak{h}$), the diagonal directions charge $0$ (the photon and the
$Z$), $E_{13}, E_{31}$ charges $\pm1$ (the charged component of the doublet) and $E_{23}, E_{32}$ charge $0$ (the neutral
component).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise determines the unbroken subalgebra by solving linear equations. It confirms that there is exactly one
unbroken direction.

::: {#exr-csd-qem-solve}
#### The unbroken subalgebra in Sage

For $X = c_1T_1 + c_2T_2 + c_3T_3 + c_4\tau$ with real $c_k$, solve $[X, \phi_1] = [X, \phi_2] = 0$ at the vacuum $\phi_+ = E_{23}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$c_1 = c_2 = 0$ and $c_3 = 2c_4$, so $X = c_4(2T_3 + \tau) = 2c_4Q_{em}$:

{{< sage exr-csd-qem-solve >}}
:::

The second exercise looks at a different point of the vacuum manifold. The unbroken generator changes, but only by a
conjugation within $H$.

::: {#exr-csd-qem-other-vacuum}
#### Another vacuum

At $\Phi = (1, 0)$, find the diagonal generators that commute with $\phi_+ = E_{13}$, and find an element $w$ of the $SU(2)$
factor of $H$ that maps $E_{23}$ to a multiple of $E_{13}$ and $Q_{em}$ to the new generator.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The generator is $Q' = \tfrac{i}{3}\operatorname{diag}(-1, 2, -1)$, and $w = e^{-\pi T_2} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ satisfies $wE_{23}w^{-1} = -E_{13}$ and $wQ_{em}w^{-1} = Q'$. Different vacua give conjugate unbroken
subgroups and physically equivalent theories:

{{< sage exr-csd-qem-other-vacuum >}}
:::

The third exercise asks for the electric charges of the fundamental representation. The answer is a curiosity of the
$\lambda_8$ embedding that was already noted in the previous chapter.

::: {#exr-csd-qem-fundamental}
#### Charges in the $\mathbf{3}$ and $\bar{\mathbf{3}}$

Give the eigenvalues of $Q_{em}/i$ on the $\mathbf{3}$ and on the $\bar{\mathbf{3}}$ of $SU(3)$, and compare them with
@exr-csd-matching-fundamental.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On the $\mathbf{3}$ the eigenvalues are the diagonal entries $\tfrac23, -\tfrac13, -\tfrac13$, those of an up-type and two
down-type quarks, as found in @exr-csd-matching-fundamental; on the $\bar{\mathbf{3}}$ they are the negatives $-\tfrac23,
\tfrac13, \tfrac13$. The charges are fractional because $Q_{em}$ is not an integer combination of the coroots of $SU(3)$;
on the adjoint, all charges are integers (@exm-csd-qem-adjoint).
:::
::::

### The Weinberg angle

The four-dimensional gauge group sits inside the simple group $SU(3)$, so its two factors have a single gauge coupling
once the generators are normalised alike. The definition below expresses this in the language of the electroweak theory
through the mixing angle of the neutral gauge bosons.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-csd-weinberg-angle}
#### Weinberg angle

Normalise the Hermitian generators of $H$ by the $SU(3)$ trace, $\tfrac12\lambda_3$ and $Y_n = \tfrac12\lambda_8$ with
$\operatorname{Tr}(Y_n^2) = \operatorname{Tr}(\tfrac14\lambda_3^2) = \tfrac12$, so that one coupling $g$ multiplies both factors. In
Standard Model conventions the doublet has hypercharge $Y = \tfrac12$ and coupling $g'$; matching $g'Y = gy_n$, where $y_n$ is
the eigenvalue of $Y_n$ on the doublet, fixes $g'$, and the **Weinberg angle** is defined by
$$
\tan\theta_W = \frac{g'}{g}, \qquad \sin^2\theta_W = \frac{g'^2}{g^2 + g'^2} .
$$ {#eq-csd-weinberg}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The hypercharge eigenvalue of the doublet is a one-line computation. The first example carries it out and finds the
coupling $g'$.

::: {#exm-csd-weinberg-yn}
#### The doublet hypercharge

$[Y_n, E_{13}] = \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt3}(1 - (-2))E_{13} = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}E_{13}$, and likewise for $E_{23}$: $y_n = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$. Then
$g' \cdot \tfrac12 = g \cdot \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ gives $g' = \sqrt3\,g$ [@manton1979].
:::

The angle itself follows from the ratio of the two couplings. The second example evaluates it and gives the electric
coupling of the unbroken $U(1)$.

::: {#exm-csd-weinberg-value}
#### $\theta_W = 60°$

$\tan\theta_W = \sqrt3$, so $\theta_W = 60°$ and $\sin^2\theta_W = \tfrac34$ (@prp-csd-weinberg); the electric coupling is $e =
gg'/\sqrt{g^2 + g'^2} = g\sin\theta_W = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}g$.
:::

The value should be compared with experiment. The third example does so, and explains why the comparison is only
qualitative.

::: {#exm-csd-weinberg-experiment}
#### Comparison with experiment

The measured value at the $Z$ mass is $\sin^2\theta_W \approx 0.23$, far from $0.75$, and $M_W/M_Z = \cos\theta_W$ is about
$0.88$, not $\tfrac12$. The model is a tree-level toy: it has no fermions (@exr-csd-matching-fermions) and fixes the angle at
the compactification scale; it shows how geometry can determine the parameters of the electroweak theory, not their
observed values.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the normalisations and the angle in Sage. It also recomputes the electric charges of the
doublet components with the Standard Model formula.

::: {#exr-csdr-weinberg}
#### The Weinberg angle in Sage

Check $\operatorname{Tr}Y_n^2 = \operatorname{Tr}T_3^2 = \tfrac12$ and $\operatorname{Tr}(Y_nT_3) = 0$ for the Hermitian generators,
compute the doublet hypercharge, $g'$ and $\sin^2\theta_W$, and the charges $Q = T_3 + Y$ of the doublet.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-csdr-weinberg >}}
:::

The second exercise obtains the angle from the masses instead of the couplings. The mass matrix of the gauge bosons
follows from the scalar kinetic term at the vacuum.

::: {#exr-csd-weinberg-masses}
#### The angle from the mass matrix

With $M^2_{ij} = -2\sum_a\operatorname{Tr}([T_i, \phi_a][T_j, \phi_a])$ at $\Phi_0$, in the basis $T_{1,2,3} = \tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_{1,2,3}$
(upper block) and $T_8 = \tfrac{i}{2}\lambda_8$, find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and read off the mixing angle of the
neutral bosons.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The eigenvalues are $\tfrac12, \tfrac12$ ($W$), $2$ ($Z$) and $0$ (photon), in units $1/R^2$. The photon is $\sin\theta\,T_3 +
\cos\theta\,T_8$ and the $Z$ is $\cos\theta\,T_3 - \sin\theta\,T_8$ with $\tan\theta = \sqrt3$: the same angle as from the couplings,
and $M_W^2/M_Z^2 = \tfrac14 = \cos^2\theta_W$:

{{< sage exr-csd-weinberg-masses >}}
:::

The third exercise checks that the angle is independent of conventions. Only the relative normalisation inside the simple
group matters.

::: {#exr-csd-weinberg-convention}
#### Independence of the hypercharge convention

Suppose the hypercharge is normalised as $Y' = cY$ with coupling $g'' = g'/c$, so that $g''Y' = g'Y$. Show that the
physical predictions $e$ and $M_W/M_Z$ are unchanged, and explain why the convention $Y = \tfrac12$ is needed only to define
$\theta_W$ in the usual way.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The covariant derivative contains only the product $g'Y$, which is unchanged, so the gauge boson mass matrix, the photon
direction and the coupling of the photon to the doublet are the same: $e = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}g$ and $M_W/M_Z = \tfrac12$. The angle
$\theta_W$ is defined as the mixing angle of the neutral bosons, $\cos\theta_W = M_W/M_Z$ at tree level; the formula $\tan\theta_W =
g'/g$ holds when $g'$ is the coupling of the generator with the doublet's hypercharge $\tfrac12$, which is the convention of
@def-csd-weinberg-angle.
:::
::::

### Worked computations

The potential and its minimum are exact polynomial identities. The first proposition collects them, as checked by the
script that draws @fig-csdr-potential.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-csd-potential}
#### The potential and its minimum

On the doublet @eq-csd-doublet, $V = -\operatorname{Tr}F_{12}^2 = \tfrac12r^2 - r + \tfrac23 = \tfrac12(r - 1)^2 + \tfrac16$ with $r = |
p|^2 + |q|^2$; its minimum value $\tfrac16$ is attained exactly on $r = 1$; and at $\Phi_0 = (0, 1)$, $F_{12} = -\tfrac12Q_{em}$, so
$V_{min} = -\tfrac14\operatorname{Tr}Q_{em}^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** The completed-square argument of @exr-csd-pp-square is the statement `potential_min`.

**Sage.** Checked by exact computation in `figures/csdr_potential.sage`.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The proposition has a direct graphical reading in the two versions of the figure. The first example relates the formula
to the static and the interactive pictures.

::: {#exm-csd-pp-graph}
#### Reading the figure

In @fig-csdr-potential the left panel is the quadratic $\tfrac12(r - 1)^2 + \tfrac16$ in $r$; as a function of $|\Phi| = \sqrt r$ it
becomes the Mexican-hat profile $\tfrac12(|\Phi|^2 - 1)^2 + \tfrac16$ of the interactive surface, with the rim at height $\tfrac16$ and
the top of the hat at $\tfrac23$.
:::

The same structure appeared in the general discussion of spontaneous symmetry breaking. The second example compares with
the potential of Part II.

::: {#exm-csd-pp-part-ii}
#### Comparison with the Mexican hat of Part II

@eq-mexican-hat, $\tfrac{\lambda}{4}(|\phi|^2 - \mu^2)^2$, has the same shape with free parameters $\lambda, \mu$ and minimum $0$. Here
both are fixed, $\lambda = 2$ and $\mu = 1$ in units of $1/R$, and there is an extra constant $\tfrac16$; the dimensionful
potential $V/(g^2R^4)$ has $\lambda_{phys} \propto g^2$ (@exr-csd-lagr-scales).
:::

The value of the potential at the minimum is a vacuum energy. The third example records what this constant means for
the four-dimensional theory.

::: {#exm-csd-pp-vacuum-energy}
#### A positive vacuum energy

$V_{min}/(g^2R^4) = \tfrac{1}{6g^2R^4} > 0$ is a positive four-dimensional cosmological constant, coming from the monopole flux
of $U(1)_{em}$ on the sphere (@exm-csd-vac-monopole). It depends on $R$, so it acts as a potential for the size of the internal
sphere, which in this rigid model is held fixed.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise proves the minimum from the completed square. It is the shortest route to the minimum
and needs no calculus.

::: {#exr-csd-pp-square}
#### The minimum from the completed square

Prove $\tfrac12r^2 - r + \tfrac23 = \tfrac12(r - 1)^2 + \tfrac16$, and deduce that the minimum over $r \geq 0$ is $\tfrac16$, attained
only at $r = 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Expanding, $\tfrac12(r - 1)^2 + \tfrac16 = \tfrac12r^2 - r + \tfrac12 + \tfrac16 = \tfrac12r^2 - r + \tfrac23$. The square is non-negative and
vanishes only at $r = 1$, which lies in the allowed range $r \geq 0$; so $V \geq \tfrac16$ with equality exactly on the sphere
$|\Phi| = 1$.
:::

The second exercise examines the profile along a ray in field space. It shows that the symmetric point is a local
maximum and the vacuum a minimum in the radial direction.

::: {#exr-csd-pp-ray}
#### Along a ray

Let $\Phi = t\Phi_0$ with $t \in \mathbb{R}$. Write $V(t)$, find its critical points and classify them.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$r = t^2$ and $V(t) = \tfrac12t^4 - t^2 + \tfrac23$, with $V'(t) = 2t^3 - 2t = 2t(t^2 - 1)$: critical points at $t = 0$ ($V'' = -2 <
0$, a local maximum with $V = \tfrac23$) and $t = \pm1$ ($V'' = 4 > 0$, minima with $V = \tfrac16$). The second derivative $4$ at
the minimum is the radial entry of the Hessian of @exr-csd-ppot-hessian.
:::

The third exercise interprets the residual field strength at the vacuum as a monopole flux. The flux is computed with the
area form of the sphere.

::: {#exr-csd-pp-flux}
#### The electromagnetic flux of the vacuum

At $\Phi_0$ the internal curvature is $F_{12}\,\theta^1 \wedge \theta^2$ with $F_{12} = -\tfrac12Q_{em}$. Writing $Q_{em} = i\,\hat Q$ with
$\hat Q = \tfrac13\operatorname{diag}(2, -1, -1)$, compute the flux $\int_{S^2}\theta^1 \wedge \theta^2$ and the field acting on a component of
electric charge $Q$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\theta^1 \wedge \theta^2 = -\sin\theta\,d\varphi \wedge d\theta = \sin\theta\,d\theta \wedge d\varphi$, the area form of the unit sphere, with
integral $4\pi$. A component of charge $Q$ (eigenvalue $iQ$ of $\operatorname{ad}Q_{em}$) feels the abelian curvature $-\tfrac{Q}{2}$
times the area form, total flux $-2\pi Q$: for the charged scalar ($Q = 1$) this is $-2\pi$, the flux of a minimal Dirac
monopole. The vacuum is the electroweak symmetry broken in the background of a magnetic monopole of $U(1)_{em}$ filling the
sphere.
:::
::::

The pattern of symmetry breaking and the masses of the gauge bosons are the second set of results. The proposition below
records them, checked by the same script.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-csd-symmetry-breaking}
#### Symmetry breaking and gauge boson masses

At $\Phi_0 = (0, 1)$ the elements of $\mathfrak{h}$ that commute with $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$ are the real multiples of $Q_{em} =
\tfrac{i}{3}\operatorname{diag}(2, -1, -1) = T_3 + \tfrac12\tau$, so $SU(2) \times U(1) \to U(1)_{em}$. In the basis $T_{1,2,3} =
\tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_{1,2,3}$, $T_8 = \tfrac{i}{2}\lambda_8$, the gauge boson mass matrix $M^2_{ij} = -2\sum_a\operatorname{Tr}([T_i,
\phi_a][T_j, \phi_a])$ (units $1/R^2$) has eigenvalues $0, \tfrac12, \tfrac12, 2$, the massless direction is $Q_{em}$, and
$M_W^2/M_Z^2 = \tfrac14$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Checked by exact computation in `figures/csdr_potential.sage`.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The charged bosons are complex combinations of the gauge fields along $T_1$ and $T_2$. The first example identifies them
and their masses.

::: {#exm-csd-psb-w}
#### The $W^\pm$ bosons

$T_1 \pm iT_2 = \tfrac{i}{2}(\sigma_1 \pm i\sigma_2)$ is proportional to $E_{12}$, respectively $E_{21}$, of charges $\pm1$ under $Q_{em}$
(@exm-csd-qem-adjoint). The real fields $W^1_\mu, W^2_\mu$ have equal masses $M_W^2 = \tfrac{1}{2R^2}$, and the combinations
$W^\pm = (W^1 \mp iW^2)/\sqrt2$ are the charged vector bosons.
:::

The neutral bosons mix, since $\Phi_0$ is charged under both $T_3$ and $T_8$. The second example writes the $Z$ and the
photon in terms of $T_3$ and $T_8$.

::: {#exm-csd-psb-neutral}
#### The $Z$ and the photon

The photon direction is $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}T_3 + \tfrac12T_8 \propto T_3 + \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}T_8 = Q_{em}$ (since $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}T_8 =
\tfrac12\tau$), and the $Z$ is the orthogonal combination $\tfrac12T_3 - \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}T_8$ with $M_Z^2 = \tfrac{2}{R^2}$. The mixing
angle is $60°$, the Weinberg angle of @exm-csd-weinberg-value.
:::

The counting of massive bosons agrees with the counting of broken generators. The third example puts the two counts
side by side.

::: {#exm-csd-psb-count}
#### Broken generators and massive bosons

$\dim H - \dim U(1)_{em} = 4 - 1 = 3$ broken generators, three massive vector bosons ($W^1, W^2, Z$) and three would-be Goldstone
directions on $S^3$ (@exm-csd-vac-flat): every broken generator gives mass to one gauge boson by eating one Goldstone
boson, as in @def-higgs-mechanism.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise counts physical degrees of freedom before and after symmetry breaking. The totals must agree, since
the breaking only reorganises the fields.

::: {#exr-csd-psb-dof}
#### Counting degrees of freedom

Count the physical degrees of freedom of the four massless gauge bosons and the complex doublet at the symmetric point,
and of the massive and massless particles at the vacuum.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Symmetric point: four massless vectors with two polarisations each, $8$, plus four real scalars: $12$. Vacuum: three massive
vectors with three polarisations, $9$, one massless photon, $2$, and one real Higgs scalar, $1$: $12$. The three
Goldstone modes have become the longitudinal polarisations of $W^\pm$ and $Z$.
:::

The second exercise computes the $\rho$ parameter of the model. This combination of masses and angle tests the doublet
nature of the Higgs field.

::: {#exr-csd-psb-rho}
#### The $\rho$ parameter

Compute $\rho = M_W^2/(M_Z^2\cos^2\theta_W)$ with the masses of the proposition and $\theta_W$ of @exm-csd-weinberg-value.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$M_W^2/M_Z^2 = \tfrac{1/2}{2} = \tfrac14$ and $\cos^2 60° = \tfrac14$, so $\rho = 1$, the tree-level value for any theory in which the
symmetry is broken by doublets. The model reproduces the electroweak mass relation exactly; only the value of the angle
is different.
:::

The third exercise shows that the photon is massless for a structural reason. The argument does not need the explicit
mass matrix.

::: {#exr-csd-psb-photon}
#### Why the photon is massless

Show that $M^2_{ij}c^j = 0$ for the coefficients $c$ of any $X = c^jT_j$ with $[X, \phi_1] = [X, \phi_2] = 0$, and deduce that
$Q_{em}$ is a zero mode of $M^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$M^2_{ij}c^j = -2\sum_a\operatorname{Tr}([T_i, \phi_a][X, \phi_a]) = 0$ when $[X, \phi_a] = 0$. Conversely, $c^iM^2_{ij}c^j = -
2\sum_a\operatorname{Tr}([X, \phi_a]^2) = 2\sum_a\|[X, \phi_a]\|^2$ vanishes only if $[X, \phi_a] = 0$. So the kernel of $M^2$ is exactly
the unbroken subalgebra, spanned by $Q_{em}$: one massless photon.
:::
::::

The Weinberg angle is the third result of the section. The proposition below records it together with the normalisations
of the generators that determine it.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-csd-weinberg}
#### The Weinberg angle of the model

The Hermitian generators $\tfrac12\lambda_3$ and $Y_n = \tfrac12\lambda_8$ satisfy $\operatorname{Tr}Y_n^2 = \operatorname{Tr}(\tfrac12\lambda_3)^2 =
\tfrac12$; $Y_n$ has eigenvalue $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ on the doublet; hence $g' = \sqrt3\,g$ and $\sin^2\theta_W = \tfrac34$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Checked by exact computation in `figures/csdr_potential.sage`.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The result depends on the normalisation of the hypercharge inside $SU(3)$. The first example explains why that
normalisation is not a choice.

::: {#exm-csd-pw-normalisation}
#### Why the normalisation is fixed

In the six-dimensional theory all generators of $SU(3)$ appear in $\operatorname{Tr}\hat F^2$ with the same coupling. A generator
normalised by $\operatorname{Tr}(X^2) = \tfrac12$ has a canonical kinetic term with coupling $g$; rescaling $Y_n$ would rescale its
coupling inversely, leaving the physics of @exr-csd-weinberg-convention unchanged. The embedding in a simple group is what
relates $g'$ to $g$.
:::

The same mechanism fixes the angle in grand unified theories, where the electroweak group also sits in a simple group.
The second example makes the comparison.

::: {#exm-csd-pw-gut}
#### A comparison with unification

In a grand unified theory the hypercharge is also a generator of a simple group, and the same argument fixes
$\sin^2\theta_W$ at the unification scale: for $SU(5)$ the value is $\tfrac38$. The CSDR model gives $\tfrac34$ because the doublet sits
differently in $SU(3)$; in both cases the low-energy value is changed by the running of the couplings.
:::

The electric charges of the doublet components follow from the same generators. The third example recomputes them with
the Standard Model formula.

::: {#exm-csd-pw-charges}
#### Charges from $Q = T_3 + Y$

With $Y = Y_n/\sqrt3 = \tfrac16\operatorname{diag}(1, 1, -2)$ the doublet has $Y = \tfrac12$, and $Q = \tfrac12\lambda_3 + Y$ gives charges
$\tfrac12 + \tfrac12 = 1$ and $-\tfrac12 + \tfrac12 = 0$ for $p$ and $q$, in agreement with @exm-csd-qem-doublet.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise derives the electric coupling of the photon. It uses only the two gauge couplings and the mixing of
the neutral bosons.

::: {#exr-csd-pw-electric}
#### The electric coupling

Show that the photon couples with strength $e = gg'/\sqrt{g^2 + g'^2}$ and evaluate it for $g' = \sqrt3\,g$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Writing $W^3 = \cos\theta_W Z + \sin\theta_W A$ and $B = -\sin\theta_W Z + \cos\theta_W A$, the coupling $gT_3W^3 + g'YB$ contains $A$ with
coefficient $g\sin\theta_W T_3 + g'\cos\theta_W Y$, which equals $e(T_3 + Y)$ when $g\sin\theta_W = g'\cos\theta_W = e$, i.e. $e =
gg'/\sqrt{g^2 + g'^2}$. For $g' = \sqrt3\,g$: $e = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}g$.
:::

The second exercise checks the trace normalisations directly by hand. These are the only inputs of the proposition besides
the eigenvalue on the doublet.

::: {#exr-csd-pw-traces}
#### The trace normalisations

Compute $\operatorname{Tr}(\tfrac12\lambda_3)^2$, $\operatorname{Tr}Y_n^2$ and $\operatorname{Tr}(\tfrac12\lambda_3Y_n)$, and the eigenvalues of $Y_n$
on the eight states of the adjoint.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\operatorname{Tr}(\tfrac12\lambda_3)^2 = \tfrac14 \cdot 2 = \tfrac12$, $\operatorname{Tr}Y_n^2 = \tfrac{1}{12}(1 + 1 + 4) = \tfrac12$, and
$\operatorname{Tr}(\tfrac12\lambda_3Y_n) = \tfrac{1}{4\sqrt3}(1 - 1 + 0) = 0$. On the adjoint, $Y_n$ has eigenvalue $y_j - y_k$ on $E_{jk}$ with
$y = \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt3}(1, 1, -2)$: $0$ on the block and the Cartan directions, $\pm\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ on the doublets, the vertical
coordinates of @fig-csdr-constraints.
:::

The third exercise asks what changes with a different embedding. The answer illustrates how strongly the embedding
determines the low-energy theory.

::: {#exr-csd-pw-other}
#### A different coset or embedding

For the $T_3$ embedding of @exm-embedding-other, is there a Weinberg angle? What would be needed in general to obtain the
electroweak structure with a different value of $\sin^2\theta_W$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With the $T_3$ embedding $H = U(1) \times U(1)$ has no $SU(2)$ factor and the scalar is a singlet; there is no electroweak
structure and no Weinberg angle. To obtain $SU(2) \times U(1)$ with a doublet one needs a centraliser containing $SU(2)$ and a
matched doublet; the angle is then fixed by the eigenvalue of the normalised $U(1)$ generator on the doublet. Larger
gauge groups and other cosets give other values, which is how realistic CSDR models were searched for [@kapetanakis1992;
@manolakos2016].
:::
::::

## Fermions and chiral zero modes {#sec-csdr-fermions}

The bosonic reduction of the previous sections has a fermionic counterpart. A spinor on $M^4 \times S^2$ in a representation
$F$ of the gauge group $G$ is symmetric when an $SU(2)$ rotation of the sphere acts on it as a gauge transformation, and at the
north pole this becomes an algebraic condition: the isotropy $U(1)$ must act trivially on the spinor and gauge indices
together. The condition keeps the components whose charge under the embedded $U(1)$ cancels the charge $\pm\tfrac12$ of the
spinor of the sphere, and the four-dimensional fermions they produce are chiral, because the gauge background is a monopole
and the index of @thm-monopole-index is not zero. This section states the constraint, solves it, and matches the result
with the zero modes computed in @sec-dirac-index: CSDR keeps exactly the zero modes that are invariant under the isometry
group. The running $\lambda_8$ model has no fermions (@exr-csd-matching-fermions), so the examples use the $T_3$ embedding of
@exm-embedding-other and the $SU(2)$ model of @exm-rules-su2. The sources are @manousselis2000 [Sec. 2, eqs. (9), (12)-(15)]
for the constraint and the rules and @dolan2009 [Secs. 2.3 and 3.2] for the symmetric spinors on the sphere, their zero modes
and their Yukawa couplings.

For more on this topic, see @hosotani2025introduction.

### The fermion constraints

The constraint compares two charges at the north pole: the charge of a component of $F$ under the embedded $U(1)$ and the
charge of a spinor component under the rotations of the tangent plane. The figure shows the first for the two embeddings of
$U(1)$ in $SU(3)$ used in this part; the second is $\pm\tfrac12$.

![Charges $q$ of the components of the $\mathbf 3$ and the $\mathbf 8$ of $SU(3)$ under the isotropy $U(1)$ of $S^2$, embedded
by $\tau = \tfrac i3\operatorname{diag}(1, 1, -2)$ (left, the running model) and by $\tau' = \tfrac i2\operatorname{diag}(1, -1, 0)$ (right,
the $T_3$ model). A component survives the fermion constraint when $|q| = \tfrac12$ (dashed lines, red points,
@prp-csf-fermion-constraint): none for $\tau$, one pair in the $\mathbf 3$ and two pairs in the $\mathbf 8$ for $\tau'$. Generated by
`figures/csf-charges.sage`.](figures/csf-charges.svg){#fig-csf-charges width=85%}

The definition is the spinor case of @def-symmetric-gauge-field. The rotation of the sphere moves the spinor and turns its
frame, and a gauge transformation is allowed to compensate.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-csf-symmetric-spinor}
#### Symmetric spinor field

Let $\psi$ be a spinor field on $M^4 \times S^2$, $S^2 = SU(2)/U(1)$, with values in a representation $F$ of the gauge group $G$, and let
$\tau: U(1) \to G$ be the embedding of @def-csdr-embedding. The field is **symmetric** if for every $s \in SU(2)$
$$
\psi(x, s\cdot y) = f(s, y)\,\Omega(s, y)\,\psi(x, y) ,
$$ {#eq-csf-symmetric-spinor}
where $\Omega(s, y)$ is the lift to spinors of the rotation of the tangent plane by $s$ (@def-spin-group) and $f(s, y) \in G$, acting in
$F$, is the compensating gauge transformation, equal to $\tau(r)$ when $s = r$ belongs to the isotropy group of $y$. Infinitesimally,
$\mathcal L_{\xi_A}\psi = F(W_A)\psi$ with the spinor Lie derivative, as in @def-symmetric-gauge-field [@manousselis2000, eq. (9);
@dolan2009, Sec. 2.3].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Without a gauge transformation the condition asks for spinors that are invariant under all rotations of the sphere. The first
example shows that there are none.

::: {#exm-csf-no-gauge}
#### No compensating gauge transformation

If $f = 1$, a symmetric spinor is an $SU(2)$-invariant section of the spinor bundle. By Frobenius reciprocity (@thm-frobenius-reciprocity)
the trivial representation occurs in the spinor fields on $S^2$ as often as the $U(1)$-charge $0$ occurs in the spinor of the sphere,
whose charges are $\pm\tfrac12$: never. The spinor harmonics of @exm-spd-spin-weighted-harmonics start at $j = \tfrac12$; without a gauge field the sphere
supports no symmetric spinor and no massless fermion (@thm-lichnerowicz-vanishing).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

With the gauge group $SU(2)$ and the embedding $\tau_1$ of @exm-rules-su2 the gauge transformation can undo the rotation of
the spinor. The second example finds the symmetric spinor.

::: {#exm-csf-su2-doublet}
#### The doublet of $SU(2)$

For $G = SU(2)$, $\tau_1(Q_3) = Q_3 = \sigma_3/2i$ and $F = \mathbf 2$, the gauge index carries charges $\mp\tfrac12$ on $e_1, e_2$, opposite to
the charges $\pm\tfrac12$ of the two spinor components: the products $e_2 \otimes S^+$ and $e_1 \otimes S^-$ are invariant. These are the
sections of the trivial bundle, constant in a suitable frame: the gauge connection cancels the spin connection, as in
@exm-spd-spin-connection-background. Two symmetric spinors, one of each internal chirality.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Symmetric spinors are the $SU(2)$-singlets among all spinor fields on the sphere. The third example states this in the language
of harmonic analysis used by @dolan2009.

::: {#exm-csf-singlets}
#### Symmetric spinors are singlets

The components of $F \otimes S$ of total charge $c$ under the isotropy $U(1)$ are sections of the homogeneous line bundle of charge $c$
(@def-homogeneous-spinor-bundle), whose sections decompose into the representations of spin $j \geq |c|$, $j - c \in \mathbb{Z}$
(@eq-spd-frobenius). Symmetric spinors are the $j = 0$ part, which exists exactly for $c = 0$ [@dolan2009, eqs. (2.38)-(2.39)]: they
are the first terms of the harmonic expansion, and every other harmonic is a massive or non-invariant mode.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The compensating transformation must be consistent along the orbit of the isotropy group. The first exercise checks this for the
embedding of @exm-csf-su2-doublet.

::: {#exr-csf-isotropy-loop}
#### The isotropy loop

The isotropy group of the north pole is $\{e^{\theta Q_3}\}$, $0 \leq \theta < 4\pi$. Show that on the spinor component of charge $s = \pm\tfrac12$ it
acts by $e^{is\theta}$, on a gauge component of charge $q$ by $e^{iq\theta}$, and that @eq-csf-symmetric-spinor at the pole requires
$e^{i(s + q)\theta}\psi_{s, q} = \psi_{s, q}$ for all $\theta$. Which products survive for $q = \pm\tfrac12$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$e^{\theta Q_3}$ fixes the pole and rotates its tangent plane by $\theta$; the spin lift acts on the component of charge $s$ by $e^{is\theta}$
(@exm-spd-spin-two), and $\tau(e^{\theta Q_3}) = e^{\theta\tau(Q_3)}$ acts by $e^{iq\theta}$, with $q$ the eigenvalue of $\tau(Q_3)/i$. Setting $s = r$ in
@eq-csf-symmetric-spinor at the pole gives $\psi = e^{i(s + q)\theta}\psi$, so $s + q = 0$ for every non-zero component. For $q = \tfrac12$ only $s =
-\tfrac12$ survives, for $q = -\tfrac12$ only $s = \tfrac12$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A field in a representation of $G$ must be a section of a bundle over the sphere. The second exercise shows that this fails
for the fundamental representation in the running model.

::: {#exr-csf-bundle}
#### When the fermion does not exist

With $\tau = \tfrac i3\operatorname{diag}(1, 1, -2)$, compute $\exp(4\pi\tau)$ and show that $\tau$ defines a homomorphism of the isotropy circle
$\{e^{\theta Q_3}\}$ into $SU(3)/\mathbb{Z}_3$ but not into $SU(3)$. Conclude that the adjoint fields of the model are well defined but
fields in the $\mathbf 3$ are not, and relate this to the Dirac quantisation $M = 2q \in \mathbb{Z}$ of @exm-spd-monopole-potential.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\exp(4\pi\tau) = \operatorname{diag}(e^{4\pi i/3}, e^{4\pi i/3}, e^{-8\pi i/3}) = e^{4\pi i/3}\mathbb 1$, a non-trivial element of the centre $\mathbb{Z}_3$, while
$e^{4\pi Q_3} = 1$. So $\theta \mapsto e^{\theta\tau}$ is well defined on the circle only modulo the centre, which acts trivially in the adjoint.
A field in the $\mathbf 3$ would have components of charge $q = \tfrac13$ and $-\tfrac23$, which see monopoles of charge $2q = \tfrac23$ and
$-\tfrac43$, not integers: there is no such line bundle, and the fermion in the $\mathbf 3$ cannot be coupled to this background at all
(@exr-csd-matching-fermions).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The charges of all small representations decide which fermions a model can have. The third exercise computes them with Sage.

::: {#exr-csf-charges}
#### Charges with Sage

With Sage, compute the charges $q$ of the weights of the $\mathbf 3$, $\mathbf 6$, $\mathbf 8$, $\mathbf{10}$ and $\mathbf{15}$ of $SU(3)$ under
$\tau' = \tfrac i2\operatorname{diag}(1, -1, 0)$, and list for each the number of components with $q = \tfrac12$ and with $q = -\tfrac12$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A weight is the triple $(h_1, h_2, h_3)$ of eigenvalues of $\operatorname{diag}(1, 0, 0)$, $\operatorname{diag}(0, 1, 0)$, $\operatorname{diag}(0, 0, 1)$
on a weight vector, and $q = \tfrac12(h_1 - h_2)$. The counts are
equal for $q = \tfrac12$ and $q = -\tfrac12$ in every representation, by the Weyl reflection exchanging $h_1$ and $h_2$:

{{< sage exr-csf-charges >}}

The $\mathbf{6}$ and the $\mathbf{10}$ have components with $|q| = \tfrac12$ as well; the representation decides the four-dimensional
gauge quantum numbers, not whether fermions exist.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

The definition becomes an algebraic condition at one point, as for the gauge field in @def-csdr-constraints. The proposition
states it and its consequence for each component of $F$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-csf-fermion-constraint}
#### The fermion constraint

A spinor field on $M^4 \times S^2$ in the representation $F$ of $G$ is symmetric if and only if it is determined by its value $\psi_0(x) =
\psi(x, y_0)$ at the north pole through @eq-csf-symmetric-spinor, and
$$
\big(\Sigma(Q_3) \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes \tau(Q_3)\big)\psi_0 = 0 ,
$$ {#eq-csf-fermion-constraint}
where $\Sigma(Q_3)$ is the spin lift of the isotropy generator, with eigenvalues $is$, $s = \mp\tfrac12$ on $S^\pm$ (with the orientation of
@exm-spd-branch-six). Decomposing $F = \bigoplus_i(q_i, h_i)$ under $U(1)_\tau \times H$, the component $(q_i, h_i)$ survives exactly
when $q_i = \pm\tfrac12$, in the spinor component of charge $s = -q_i$ [@manousselis2000, eqs. (12)-(13); @dolan2009, eqs. (2.38)-(2.39)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In the running model of this part nothing survives. The first example records the reason, which is the content of
@exr-csd-matching-fermions.

::: {#exm-csf-lambda8}
#### The running model has no fermions

For $\tau = \tfrac i3\operatorname{diag}(1, 1, -2)$ every charge is a multiple of $\tfrac13$, and $\pm\tfrac12$ never occurs
(@fig-csf-charges): a reduction of pure Yang-Mills theory with $G = SU(3)$ over $S^2$ has a Higgs doublet but no fermion. Adding
fermions requires a different gauge group or embedding, and the fundamental representation is not even allowed
(@exr-csf-bundle).
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

The $T_3$ embedding gives charges $\pm\tfrac12$ in the fundamental representation. The second example finds the surviving
components of a fermion in the $\mathbf 3$.

::: {#exm-csf-t3-fundamental}
#### The $\mathbf 3$ in the $T_3$ model

For $\tau' = \tfrac i2\operatorname{diag}(1, -1, 0)$, $e_1$ has $q = \tfrac12$, $e_2$ has $q = -\tfrac12$ and $e_3$ has $q = 0$ (@fig-csf-charges). The
constraint keeps $e_1 \otimes S^+$ and $e_2 \otimes S^-$ and removes $e_3$ entirely. The centraliser $H = U(1)_3 \times U(1)_8$ of @exm-embedding-other
acts on $e_1$, $e_2$ with the charges $(t, y) = (\tfrac12, 1)$ and $(-\tfrac12, 1)$, where $t$ is the eigenvalue of $\tfrac12\operatorname{diag}(1, -1, 0)$
and $y$ that of $\operatorname{diag}(1, 1, -2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Gauginos are fermions in the adjoint representation of the gauge group. The third example finds which of them survive in the $T_3$ model.

::: {#exm-csf-adjoint}
#### The adjoint in the $T_3$ model

On the matrix unit $E_{jk}$ the charge is $t_j - t_k$ with $t = (\tfrac12, -\tfrac12, 0)$: $\pm1$ on $E_{12}$, $E_{21}$; $\tfrac12$ on $E_{13}$, $E_{32}$; $-\tfrac12$ on
$E_{31}$, $E_{23}$; $0$ on the Cartan subalgebra. Four components survive: $E_{13}$, $E_{32}$ with $S^+$ and $E_{31}$, $E_{23}$ with $S^-$, with
$H$-charges $(t, y) = (\tfrac12, 3), (\tfrac12, -3), (-\tfrac12, -3), (-\tfrac12, 3)$. The gauginos of $H$ itself (charge $0$) do not survive.
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The constraint is a statement about invariants of the isotropy group. The first exercise rederives it from the infinitesimal
form of the definition.

::: {#exr-csf-infinitesimal}
#### From the Lie derivative

For a Killing vector $\xi$ the spinor Lie derivative is $\mathcal L_\xi\psi = \nabla_\xi\psi - \tfrac14(\nabla_a\xi_b)\gamma^a\gamma^b\psi$. At the north pole the
Killing vector $\xi_3$ of the isotropy generator vanishes. Show that the infinitesimal condition $\mathcal L_{\xi_3}\psi = F(W_3)\psi$ then contains
no derivative of $\psi$ and is the derivative at $\theta = 0$ of the condition of @exr-csf-isotropy-loop, and that the conditions for $\xi_1$, $\xi_2$
impose nothing on $\psi_0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
At a zero of $\xi_3$ the term $\nabla_{\xi_3}\psi$ vanishes, and $-\tfrac14(\nabla_a\xi_b)\gamma^a\gamma^b$ is the generator of the rotation of the tangent
plane that $\xi_3$ induces, lifted to spinors: its eigenvalues on the components of charge $s$ are proportional to $is$. The compensating
parameter $W_3$ at the pole generates $\tau$ restricted to the isotropy group. Both sides are therefore the generators of the two
actions in @exr-csf-isotropy-loop, and the condition is the derivative at $\theta = 0$ of $e^{i(s + q)\theta}\psi_{s, q} = \psi_{s, q}$, that is
$(s + q)\psi_{s, q} = 0$, @eq-csf-fermion-constraint. The vectors $\xi_1$, $\xi_2$ do not vanish at the pole: their conditions express
$\nabla_{\xi_a}\psi$ through $\psi$, determining $\psi$ along the sphere from $\psi_0$ without constraining $\psi_0$ [@manousselis2000, eq. (9)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For $SU(2)$ and the embeddings $\tau_n$ the charges are multiples of $n$. The second exercise finds which representations
contain fermions.

::: {#exr-csf-su2-tau-n}
#### $SU(2)$ with $\tau_n$

For $G = SU(2)$, $\tau_n(Q_3) = nQ_3$ and $F$ the representation of spin $j$, the charges are $-nm$, $m = -j, \dots, j$. For which $(n, j)$ do
fermions survive, and how many components? Check the answer with Sage for $1 \leq n \leq 4$ and $j \leq 3$, and compare with the scalars, which
need charges $\pm1$ (@exm-rules-su2).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$nm = \pm\tfrac12$ requires $|n| = 1$ and $m = \pm\tfrac12$, so $j$ must be a half-integer, and then exactly two components survive, $m = \tfrac12$ and $m
= -\tfrac12$:

{{< sage exr-csf-su2-tau-n >}}

 For $|n| \geq 2$ no fermion survives in any representation, as no scalar does (@exm-rules-su2): $\tau_1$ is the only embedding
with matter, and it carries both a scalar (in the adjoint) and fermions (in half-integer spins).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The literature states the rule as a matching of identical representations of the isotropy group. The third exercise compares
this with @eq-csf-fermion-constraint.

::: {#exr-csf-matching-rule}
#### Identical or conjugate

The rule of @manousselis2000 [eqs. (12)-(13)] keeps an $h_i$ multiplet for each pair of identical $R$-representations in $F$ and in the
spinor of $SO(d)$. Show that for $R = U(1)$ on $S^2$ it keeps the same components of $F$ as @prp-csf-fermion-constraint, and that the two
formulations differ only in which spinor component is attached to which charge, that is, in the name of the internal chirality.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The spinor of $SO(2)$ contains both charges $\pm\tfrac12$, so "$q_i$ equals a spinor charge" and "$q_i$ is minus a spinor charge" both select
$q_i = \pm\tfrac12$. The first attaches $q_i = \tfrac12$ to the spinor component of charge $\tfrac12$, the second to that of charge $-\tfrac12$:
the two differ by complex conjugation of the spinor representation, which exchanges $S^+$ and $S^-$ on $S^2$. The four-dimensional
chiralities are therefore exchanged between the two conventions, and every statement about chirality must be made with one of them;
this part uses the invariance $s + q = 0$, which is what the index computation of @thm-monopole-index also uses.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

### Solving the constraints

Each surviving component of $F$ gives one four-dimensional Weyl fermion, whose chirality is fixed by the internal chirality of its
spinor component. The proposition collects the result for a six-dimensional Weyl fermion.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-csf-chiral-content}
#### Four-dimensional fermions from $S^2$

Let $\psi$ be a six-dimensional Weyl spinor of positive chirality in the representation $F = \bigoplus_i(q_i, h_i)$ of $G$, reduced over
$S^2$ with the embedding $\tau$. Its symmetric part is a set of four-dimensional massless Weyl fermions: a right-handed one in $h_i$ for
each component with $q_i = \tfrac12$, and a left-handed one in $h_i$ for each component with $q_i = -\tfrac12$. The four-dimensional theory is
chiral unless the left-handed representations $h_i$ ($q_i = -\tfrac12$) are the conjugates of the right-handed ones ($q_i = \tfrac12$). The Higgs
fields couple to them through the internal Dirac operator, with Yukawa couplings fixed by the reduction [@manousselis2000, eqs. (14)-(15),
(20)-(21); @dolan2009, Sec. 3.2, eq. (3.13)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The $SU(2)$ model is the smallest example with a chiral result. The first example reads off its four-dimensional fermions and their charges.

::: {#exm-csf-su2-content}
#### The $SU(2)$ model

With $\tau_1$ and $F = \mathbf 2$ (@exm-csf-su2-doublet), $H = U(1)$ is generated by $\tau_1(Q_3)$ itself, so the $H$-charge of a component is
its $q$: $e_2$ ($q = \tfrac12$) gives a right-handed fermion of charge $\tfrac12$ and $e_1$ ($q = -\tfrac12$) a left-handed one of charge $-\tfrac12$.
Since a right-handed fermion of charge $\tfrac12$ is equivalent to a left-handed one of charge $-\tfrac12$ (@prp-dq-charge-conjugation), the
spectrum is two left-handed fermions of charge $-\tfrac12$: chiral.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In the $T_3$ model the fundamental representation gives two fermions with different charges under the second $U(1)$. The second
example lists them.

::: {#exm-csf-t3-content}
#### The $T_3$ model with a fermion in the $\mathbf 3$

From @exm-csf-t3-fundamental: a right-handed fermion with $(t, y) = (\tfrac12, 1)$ and a left-handed one with $(-\tfrac12, 1)$. In left-handed
form the charges are $(-\tfrac12, -1)$ and $(-\tfrac12, 1)$, which are not closed under $(t, y) \to (-t, -y)$: the spectrum is chiral, and the
$U(1)_3$ charges, both $-\tfrac12$, are those of a chiral $U(1)$ (@exr-csf-anomaly).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The adjoint representation is real, and one might expect a non-chiral result from it. The third example shows that the
reduction is chiral all the same.

::: {#exm-csf-t3-adjoint-content}
#### Gauginos of the $T_3$ model

From @exm-csf-adjoint, the right-handed fermions have $(t, y) = (\tfrac12, \pm3)$ and the left-handed ones $(-\tfrac12, \mp3)$; in left-handed form
the four are $2 \times (-\tfrac12, 3) + 2 \times (-\tfrac12, -3)$. Every left-handed fermion has $t = -\tfrac12$, so the spectrum is chiral under $U(1)_3$
although $F$ is real: the chirality comes from the monopole background, not from the representation.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
A chiral spectrum of abelian charges must satisfy the anomaly conditions of @def-anomaly to be consistent. The first exercise
computes the anomalies of the $T_3$ model with Sage.

::: {#exr-csf-anomaly}
#### Anomalies of the $T_3$ model

With Sage, compute $\sum t^3$, $\sum y^3$, $\sum t^2y$, $\sum ty^2$, $\sum t$ and $\sum y$ over the left-handed fermions of @exm-csf-t3-content and of
@exm-csf-t3-adjoint-content. Which are anomalous, and what does this say about the six-dimensional theory?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For the $\mathbf 3$: $\sum t^3 = -\tfrac14$, $\sum t = -1$, $\sum ty^2 = -1$, the others $0$; for the adjoint: $\sum t^3 = -\tfrac12$, $\sum t = -2$, $\sum ty^2 =
-18$, the others $0$:

{{< sage exr-csf-anomaly >}}

Both are anomalous. A single six-dimensional Weyl fermion in a representation of $SU(3)$ has a six-dimensional gauge anomaly, and the
four-dimensional anomaly of its zero modes is its trace; a consistent model needs an anomaly-free fermion content in the higher
dimension, as for $E_8$ in ten dimensions [@manousselis2000, eq. (16)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Weyl condition in six dimensions is what makes the result chiral. The second exercise drops it and finds a vector-like spectrum.

::: {#exr-csf-dirac-six}
#### A six-dimensional Dirac fermion

Repeat @prp-csf-chiral-content for a six-dimensional Dirac fermion, the sum of Weyl fermions of both chiralities in the same representation
$F$, and show that the four-dimensional spectrum is always vector-like.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The Weyl spinor of negative chirality is $(\psi_L \otimes S^+) \oplus (\psi_R \otimes S^-)$ (@prp-spinor-branching). A component with $q_i = \tfrac12$
pairs with $S^+$ in both, giving $\psi_R$ from the positive and $\psi_L$ from the negative chirality, both in $h_i$: a Dirac fermion. The same holds
for $q_i = -\tfrac12$. Every surviving multiplet is a Dirac fermion, and chirality needs the six-dimensional Weyl condition
[@manousselis2000, eqs. (14)-(15)], the analogue of @prp-kkf-vectorlike.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Yukawa couplings link the fermions to the Higgs field of the same model. The third exercise checks that the charges allow
them in the $SU(2)$ model.

::: {#exr-csf-yukawa}
#### A Yukawa coupling

In the $SU(2)$ model with $\tau_1$ the Higgs field is the complex scalar of @exm-rules-su2, in the components $E_{12}$, $E_{21}$ of the adjoint, of
$H$-charges $\pm1$. Show that a term $\psi_L^T\epsilon\,\psi_L\,\phi$ built from the two left-handed fermions of @exm-csf-su2-content is invariant
for one of the two components, and that it is the coupling of @dolan2009 [eq. (3.13)] for $m = 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The two left-handed fermions have $H$-charge $-\tfrac12$ each, so the bilinear has charge $-1$ and the term is invariant with the component of
charge $+1$. In @dolan2009 the case $m = 1$ has the charges $p = \pm1$, the symmetric spinors are the constants of the trivial bundle, and the
term (3.13), built from the Higgs field $\phi$ and the two symmetric spinors, survives exactly for odd $m$ [@dolan2009, Sec. 3.2]: the
Yukawa coupling of the zero modes comes from the internal components $\phi_a$ in the Dirac operator (@prp-csf-chiral-content).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Chiral zero modes and the index

The surviving fermions are zero modes of the internal Dirac operator twisted by the monopole background. The figure counts the
zero modes of a component of charge $q$ and marks the ones that CSDR keeps.

![Zero modes on $S^2$ of a spinor component of isotropy charge $q$, which sees the monopole of charge $M = 2q$: $|2q|$ zero modes (bars;
red: internal chirality $+1$, pairing with right-handed four-dimensional spinors in a six-dimensional Weyl spinor of positive
chirality; blue: $-1$), forming the representation of spin $|q| - \tfrac12$ of $SU(2)$. The stars mark the $SU(2)$-invariant zero modes, the
symmetric spinors kept by CSDR, which exist only for $|q| = \tfrac12$ (@prp-csf-index-match). The counts are checked from the regular
solutions of the zero-mode equation of @exm-spd-zero-mode-solution. Generated by `figures/csf-index.sage`.](figures/csf-index.svg){#fig-csf-index width=70%}

{{< interactive csf-index 460 >}}

The background gauge field seen by a component of charge $q$ is the canonical connection of $SU(2) \to S^2$ in the charge $q$, a monopole.
The proposition matches the CSDR fermions with the zero modes of @thm-monopole-index.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-csf-index-match}
#### CSDR fermions and the index

On the component $(q, h)$ of $F$, the internal Dirac operator of the CSDR background is the twisted Dirac operator of the monopole of charge
$M = 2q$ (@def-twisted-dirac-operator, in the conventions of @exr-spd-spin-connection-charge). It has $|2q|$ zero modes, of internal chirality
$\operatorname{sign}q$, forming the representation of spin $|q| - \tfrac12$ of the isometry group $SU(2)$ (@thm-monopole-index). The symmetric
spinors of @prp-csf-fermion-constraint are exactly the $SU(2)$-invariant zero modes, which exist if and only if $|q| = \tfrac12$. Summed over $F$,
the index is $\sum_i 2q_i\dim h_i = 2\operatorname{tr}_F(\tau(Q_3)/i) = 0$ for semisimple $G$, while the net chirality of the CSDR fermions is $\sum_{|q_i| =
1/2}2q_i\dim h_i$, which need not vanish [@dolan2009, eqs. (2.45)-(2.47)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For the $SU(2)$ model the matching can be followed component by component. The first example does this for a fermion in the
representation of spin $\tfrac32$.

::: {#exm-csf-index-su2}
#### Spin $\tfrac32$ of $SU(2)$

With $\tau_1$ and $F$ of spin $\tfrac32$, the charges are $q = -m = \pm\tfrac12, \pm\tfrac32$. The components $q = \pm\tfrac32$ see $M = \pm3$ and have three zero
modes each, a triplet of the isometry $SU(2)$; the components $q = \pm\tfrac12$ have one zero mode each, a singlet. The index is $3 + 1 - 1 - 3 = 0$;
CSDR keeps the two singlets, one right-handed and one left-handed, with $H$-charges $\tfrac12$ and $-\tfrac12$, that is two left-handed fermions of
charge $-\tfrac12$, as for the doublet.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In the $T_3$ model the adjoint contains components of charge $\pm1$ as well as $\pm\tfrac12$. The second example counts all zero modes.

::: {#exm-csf-index-t3}
#### All zero modes of the $T_3$ adjoint

$E_{12}$ ($q = 1$, $M = 2$) has two zero modes of chirality $+1$, a doublet of $SU(2)$; $E_{21}$ has two of chirality $-1$; the four components with
$q = \pm\tfrac12$ have one each; the Cartan components have none (@thm-lichnerowicz-vanishing). The index is $2 - 2 + 1 + 1 - 1 - 1 = 0$, and CSDR keeps
the four singlets of @exm-csf-adjoint, whose net $U(1)_3$-chirality is not zero (@exm-csf-t3-adjoint-content).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The zero modes that CSDR drops are massless too. The third example says what they are and why the truncation keeps the
theory consistent.

::: {#exm-csf-dropped-modes}
#### The zero modes that are not kept

The doublet of zero modes of $E_{12}$ in @exm-csf-index-t3 consists of massless four-dimensional fermions that transform as a doublet under the
isometry $SU(2)$ combined with gauge transformations. CSDR keeps the singlets of this group, and a truncation to singlets is consistent: the
equations of motion of the singlets do not source the doublets (@prp-csdr-rules-text, symmetric criticality). The full massless spectrum
of the six-dimensional theory is larger, and @dolan2009 [eqs. (2.45)-(2.47)] keeps all of it in the equivariant reduction.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The count of zero modes can be checked by solving the zero-mode equation. The first exercise does it with Sage for several
charges.

::: {#exr-csf-zero-mode-count}
#### Counting the zero modes

Using the solutions $g = \sin^{-m - 1/2}\tfrac\theta2\cos^{m + M - 1/2}\tfrac\theta2$ of @exm-spd-zero-mode-solution, count with Sage the regular ones for
$M = 2q$, $q = \tfrac12, 1, \tfrac32, 2$, check that each solves the zero-mode equation, and list their $U(1)$ charges $m$. Which value of $m$ belongs to
the $SU(2)$ singlet when $q = \tfrac12$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Regularity requires $-m - \tfrac12 \geq 0$ and $m + M - \tfrac12 \geq 0$, which leaves $m = -\tfrac12, \dots, \tfrac12 - M$, that is $M = 2q$ values:

{{< sage exr-csf-zero-mode-count >}}

For $q = \tfrac12$ the single solution has $m = -\tfrac12$ and $g = 1$: it is the constant spinor of @exm-csf-su2-doublet, the gauge charge
cancelling the spin charge.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The index of the whole representation vanishes for a semisimple group. The second exercise tabulates zero modes, index and CSDR
fermions for several representations of $SU(3)$ with Sage.

::: {#exr-csf-index-table}
#### A table for the $T_3$ model

With Sage, for the $\mathbf 3$, $\mathbf 6$, $\mathbf 8$ and $\mathbf{10}$ of $SU(3)$ with $\tau'$, list the numbers of zero modes of each internal chirality, the
index, and the numbers of right- and left-handed CSDR fermions.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Each component of charge $q$ contributes $|2q|$ zero modes of chirality $\operatorname{sign}q$ and one CSDR fermion when $|q| = \tfrac12$:

{{< sage exr-csf-index-table >}}

The index vanishes in every case, since $\tau'$ is traceless; the CSDR fermions are equal in number for the two chiralities, but their $H$-charges
differ, so the spectra are chiral in the sense of @prp-csf-chiral-content.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The massive modes come in Dirac pairs with masses set by the radius. The third exercise finds the lightest of them for the
components that have a zero mode.

::: {#exr-csf-massive}
#### The first massive level

Using the eigenvalues $k(k + |M|)/R^2$ of $D_A^2$ on a sphere of radius $R$ (@thm-monopole-index), find the mass of the lightest massive
four-dimensional fermion from a component with $q = \tfrac12$ and from one with $q = 0$, and compare with the masses of the Higgs and gauge
bosons of the model, which are of order $1/R$ (@exr-csd-int-higgs-mass).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $q = \tfrac12$, $|M| = 1$ and $k = 1$ give $\sqrt2/R$; for $q = 0$ the untwisted spectrum $(j + \tfrac12)^2/R^2$ gives $1/R$
(@thm-sphere-dirac-spectrum). Both are of the order of the Higgs and $W$ masses $\sqrt2/R$ and $1/(\sqrt2R)$: the massive fermions are not
separated from the four-dimensional theory by a large gap, and the reduced theory is a truncation, not a low-energy limit, unless the
radius is small and the electroweak scale is produced in another way.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
