### Exercises

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The exercises of this part combine the constraint, the four-dimensional content and the index. Each goes from a six-dimensional
model to its four-dimensional fermions by two routes.

The $T_3$ model has a scalar and fermions. The first integrative exercise puts them together.

::: {#exr-csf-int-t3-model}
#### The $T_3$ model with matter

Take six-dimensional $SU(3)$ Yang-Mills theory with a Weyl fermion of positive chirality in the $\mathbf 3$, reduced over $S^2$ with $\tau'$. Give
the four-dimensional gauge group, the scalar (@exr-csd-int-t3-model), the fermions with their charges, and decide whether a Yukawa coupling of
the scalar to the two fermions is allowed by the charges; check the charges with Sage from the matrices.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$H = U(1)_3 \times U(1)_8$; the scalar is $f$ in $E_{12}$, with $(t, y) = (1, 0)$; the fermions are $\psi_R$ with $(\tfrac12, 1)$ and $\psi_L$ with $(-\tfrac12, 1)$
(@exm-csf-t3-content). The Dirac bilinear $\bar\psi_L\psi_R$ has charge $(\tfrac12, 1) - (-\tfrac12, 1) = (1, 0)$, so $f^*\bar\psi_L\psi_R$ is invariant:

{{< sage exr-csf-int-t3-model >}}

The model has
a Yukawa coupling, and in the vacuum $|f| = 1$ it gives the two fermions a Dirac mass of order $1/R$, breaking $U(1)_3$ together with the
chirality.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The isometry group of the sphere organises all zero modes, not only those that CSDR keeps. The second integrative exercise counts
both for the adjoint of the $T_3$ model.

::: {#exr-csf-int-all-modes}
#### Kept and dropped modes

For the gaugino of the $T_3$ model, list all massless four-dimensional fermions of the full Kaluza-Klein reduction with their $SU(2)$
representations and $H$-charges, and separate those kept by CSDR. Check the net $U(1)_3$-chirality of each set.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Full reduction: $E_{12}$ gives a right-handed $SU(2)$-doublet with $(t, y) = (1, 0)$, $E_{21}$ a left-handed doublet with $(-1, 0)$, and the four
singlets of @exm-csf-adjoint (@exm-csf-index-t3). In left-handed form the doublets are $2 \times 2$ fermions with $t = -1$, and the singlets $4$ fermions
with $t = -\tfrac12$. CSDR keeps the singlets. The index in each set vanishes when the chiralities are counted with their sign, since the sum of
$2q$ over each set is $0$; the CSDR spectrum is chiral in its $H$-charges (@exm-csf-t3-adjoint-content).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The circle and the sphere can be compared directly. The third integrative exercise explains why one gives chiral fermions and
the other does not.

::: {#exr-csf-int-circle-sphere}
#### Circle versus sphere

Compare the reduction of a fermion on $M^4 \times S^1$ (@prp-kkf-vectorlike) with the reduction on $M^4 \times S^2$ with a monopole
background (@prp-csf-chiral-content): the existence of a chirality operator on the internal space, the index, and the role of the gauge
background. Which ingredient would make the circle chiral?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On $S^1$ the internal space is odd-dimensional, there is no internal chirality, every zero mode gives a Dirac fermion and no background on the
circle can change this (@exr-spd-nogo-odd). On $S^2$ the internal chirality exists, the index of the twisted operator is the monopole charge
(@thm-monopole-index), and the background makes the zero modes of one chirality; CSDR keeps the invariant ones. The circle becomes chiral only when
the reflection $y \to -y$ is imposed as a projection, the orbifold $S^1/\mathbb{Z}_2$ of @prp-kkf-orbifold-zero-mode, which removes one internal
chirality by hand rather than through an index.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

## Exercises {#sec-four-dimensional-theory-exercises}

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Three exercises that combine the two sections: the Higgs mass predicted by the model, the complete analysis of the
$T_3$ embedding, and a survey of the whole reduction from six to four dimensions.

The masses of the Higgs boson and of the gauge bosons are all determined by $g$ and $R$. The first integrative exercise
computes them and finds a parameter-free ratio.

::: {#exr-csd-int-higgs-mass}
#### The Higgs mass

Using @eq-csd-reduced-lagrangian, compute the tree-level Higgs mass from the radial fluctuation $\Phi = (0, 1 + \rho)$ and
compare it with $M_W$ and $M_Z$ of @prp-csd-symmetry-breaking. Check the result in Standard Model language with $H =
\Phi/(gR)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The kinetic term of $\rho$ is $\tfrac{1}{g^2R^2}(\partial\rho)^2$ (@exm-csd-lagr-kinetic) and the potential $\tfrac{1}{g^2R^4}(\tfrac16 +
2\rho^2 + \dots)$, so $m_H^2 = \tfrac{2/(g^2R^4)}{1/(g^2R^2)} = \tfrac{2}{R^2}$. With $M_W^2 = \tfrac{1}{2R^2}$ and $M_Z^2 = \tfrac{2}{R^2}$:
$m_H = 2M_W = M_Z$, a prediction independent of $g$ and $R$. In Standard Model language, $v^2 = \tfrac{2}{g^2R^2}$ and $\lambda =
\tfrac{g^2}{2}$ (@exr-csd-lagr-scales) give $m_H^2 = 2\lambda v^2$ and $M_W^2 = \tfrac14g^2v^2$, the same values:

{{< sage exr-csd-int-higgs-mass >}}
:::

The alternative embedding of the previous chapter gives a different four-dimensional theory. The second integrative
exercise derives it completely, from the constraints to the vacuum.

::: {#exr-csd-int-t3-model}
#### The $T_3$ model in full

For $\tau' = \tfrac{i}{2}\operatorname{diag}(1, -1, 0)$, solve the constraints, compute $F_{12}$ and $V$, find the vacuum and the
unbroken group, and compare with the $\lambda_8$ model.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The $+i$ eigenspace is $\operatorname{span}(E_{12})$, so $\phi_+ = fE_{12}$: one complex singlet. Then $F_{12} = \tfrac{i}{2}(|f|^2 -
1)\operatorname{diag}(1, -1, 0)$ and $V = \tfrac12(|f|^2 - 1)^2$, minimised at $|f| = 1$ with $V = 0$ and $F_{12} = 0$: the vacuum is
flat. The vacuum breaks the $U(1)$ generated by $T_3$ (under which $f$ has charge $1$), and the $U(1)$ generated by $\lambda_8$
survives. Unlike the $\lambda_8$ model, the vacuum energy vanishes, because $\tau'$ extends to the embedding of all of
$SU(2)$ in the upper block (@exr-csd-pot-compare):

{{< sage exr-csd-int-t3-model >}}
:::

The last exercise reviews the whole construction of the two chapters. It traces each four-dimensional quantity back to
the data of the reduction.

::: {#exr-csd-int-survey}
#### From six dimensions to the electroweak theory

List the data of the model (coset, gauge group, embedding) and, for each of the following, the step of the two chapters
that determines it: the gauge group $SU(2) \times U(1)$, the Higgs doublet, the shape of the potential, the vacuum, the
unbroken $U(1)_{em}$, $\sin^2\theta_W$, $m_H/M_W$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Data: $S^2 = SU(2)/U(1)$, $G = SU(3)$, $\tau(Q_3) = \tfrac{i}{3}\operatorname{diag}(1, 1, -2)$. The gauge group is the centraliser of
$\tau$ (@def-csdr-centraliser, @prp-csdr-eigenspaces); the doublet is the $+i$ eigenspace matched with the tangent space
(@prp-csd-sphere-matching, @prp-csd-doublet-solution); the potential is $-\operatorname{Tr}F_{12}^2$ with $F_{12} = [\phi_1, \phi_2] -
\tau$, its shape fixed by the structure constant $f_{12}{}^3$ and the embedding (@prp-csd-potential); the vacuum is the sphere
$|\Phi| = 1$; the unbroken group is the stabiliser of $\Phi_0$, generated by $Q_{em} = T_3 + \tfrac12\tau$
(@prp-csd-symmetry-breaking); $\sin^2\theta_W = \tfrac34$ comes from the normalisation of $\tau$ inside $SU(3)$
(@prp-csd-weinberg); and $m_H = 2M_W$ from the relative normalisation of the potential and kinetic terms in
@eq-csd-reduced-lagrangian (@exr-csd-int-higgs-mass). The only free parameters are $g$ and $R$, and every dimensionless
ratio is fixed.
:::
::::
